Instagram announced a change on Monday that may spell the end for users being nudged to visit a creator’s “link in bio.” At least when they’re promoting products sold on Amazon .
Starting today, creators and businesses can attach multiple Amazon affiliate links to their Instagram content—up to 30 per video or 20 per regular feed post. ( Affiliate links let creators earn a commission on any resulting sales.) To participate in this Amazon program, creators must be US-based adults with a professional account that has over 1,000 followers.
Instagram’s parent company, Meta , dropped this shopping-focused change right before the holiday season really kicks off. As creators look to cash in on Amazon's sales, you might expect an avalanche of affiliate posts as you sip hot cocoa and scroll through Reels. But Instagram claims this won’t be the case.
“We don’t expect a sudden influx of shopping content from this launch,” Instagram spokesperson Megan Buckley tells WIRED. “Instagram’s recommendation systems will continue to recommend content based on people’s interests and what we think they’ll enjoy and find valuable. This update makes creators’ product recommendations easier to shop.”
For years, Instagram users could attach a single external link to their bio information. This led to the rise of bundlers like Linktree, where creators could create simple one-page sites with multiple links to content, like shopping recommendations or news articles. In 2023, Instagram expanded the number of links allowed in profiles to five. This most recent update could change how it feels to scroll Instagram, moving more shopping nudges from Amazon storefronts hidden in the bio to direct links on the viral videos.
In an example shared by Meta, a woman recording a Reel leans into her camera as she applies makeup. The caption reads: “My favorite lip tint these days!” Above the creator’s name, a small image tile pops up with the Amazon product. Tap the product and a page opens inside Instagram with the price. Tap one of the listed items, and Instagram will bump you over to the Amazon app or website to complete your purchase.
This change comes as social media shopping habits continue to expand and evolve. TikTok , one of Meta’s primary competitors, has been quite successful in expanding users’ purchasing habits through the app. Around this time last year, an analytics firm estimated that $19 billion worth of products were sold globally through TikTok Shop, putting it at roughly the same size as eBay. Unlike TikTok, however, Instagram will not take a cut of the sales (at least for now). Reddit is also experimenting with how users shop, heading into this holiday season, recently announcing Reddit Reviews , which uses generative AI to summarize user sentiment about products.
For over a decade, Instagram developers have searched for ways to streamline how users spend money through the app. In 2016, WIRED wrote about how the social media app added select commerce links from brands like Warby Parker, a fairly novel attempt at the time to get people to buy stuff through social media. A few years later, the Instagram experience morphed into something like a “ digital mall ” with in-app checkouts.
This latest attempt moves links from creator bios and places them directly in users' feeds. While this could be a boon for creators, the platform’s implementation could annoy users, who are already inundated with ads online. We’ll see if this change clicks.

US President Donald Trump said on Monday that he may meet with North Korean Supreme Leader Kim Jong-un in China this week.
Trump made the comments while speaking to reporters as he departed the White House to begin his trip to Asia, which will see him arrive in the Philippines early on Tuesday.
The president is then set to travel on to China, where he is scheduled to take part in trilateral talks with his Russian and Chinese counterparts Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping.
"We may meet with Kim Jong-un also," Trump told the media. "So that would be good. We have the chance to accomplish a lot."
Trump is planning to discuss nuclear disarmament when he meets with Putin and Xi in Shenzhen in southeastern China this week, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.
"We're going to talk about denuclearisation. Tough subject because it's very hard for any of us say we'll get rid of our nukes," Trump said on Monday. "Especially since you do have other countries."
He added that the wars in Iran and Ukraine would also come up, as well as "economics and trade."
In August, Trump talked up his relationship with Kim and said the pair would meet at some point in the year, although he gave no further details.
"The fact that I get along with him, that's a good thing not a bad thing. He has 57 very powerful nuclear weapons. Should have never allowed it to happen," the president said at the time, adding: "If I were president, I wouldn't have allowed it. But he's got them."
The director general of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), Rafael Grossi, said in September that the reported expansion of North Korea's production of weapons-grade nuclear material was a "cause for serious concern."

In a joint statement, 47 aid, trade union and rights groups urged ‌the five countries to ​abandon the Rwanda plan.
Five European countries have announced a plan to send rejected asylum seekers to a processing centre in Rwanda as early as next year, drawing condemnation from rights groups who said it would leave vulnerable people at risk of abuse.
The planned scheme, which is still being negotiated with Rwanda, would send people to a centre where the migrants could choose to return home, settle or go somewhere else where they had a right to stay, Kigali said on Monday.
Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands said that the plan aimed to deter more people from migrating to Europe. The European Union has worked for years to tighten migration rules, reduce the number of asylum seekers arriving and increase deportations of migrants who are not entitled to stay.
“I think this will be a game changer, making us able to confront the massive challenges with illegal migration,” Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said. “We will break down the business model of human smugglers. We will take back control of our borders and we will remove the incentives for illegal migration.”
Rwanda’s interior minister, Vincent Biruta, said his country would give a “second chance” to people who have no right to stay in Europe.
He added that arrivals would be able “to voluntarily return to the countries of origin, integrate into Rwandan society or relocate to another destination where they have the legal right to reside, according to their preference”.
When asked how Kigali would ensure refugees’ human rights, Biruta said, “There will be an independent monitoring mechanism” and that it would cooperate with the United Nations’ refugee agency.
Human rights groups criticised the plans, saying that EU countries could not guarantee their rights would be respected there.
In a joint statement, 47 aid, trade union and rights groups urged ‌the five countries to abandon the Rwanda plan — echoing criticisms of a different migration settlement plan between Britain and Rwanda in the early 2020s.
The plan “signals that Member States accept the risk of serious human rights violations against one of the most marginalized groups in society, in return for a deterrence goal that evidence clearly suggests they will not reach,” read the statement from the International Rescue Committee, the Dutch Council for Refugees and other groups.
A Human Rights Watch researcher said the deal “would finance and provide political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad”.
Germany’s interior minister said the European plan was not comparable to a scrapped 2022 deal with the United Kingdom because only those whose asylum claims are rejected will be sent to Rwanda.
The UK’s Supreme Court ruled that the 2022 deal was unlawful because Rwanda was not considered a safe third country to which migrants could be sent.

November is here, the holidays are approaching, and it’s gotten cold outside—the perfect time of year to cozy up inside with some of the best films gracing streaming services.
This month, there’s plenty of Halloween hangover for horror fans, with viral sensation Backrooms making corridors and empty rooms unimaginably spooky on HBO Max, Thanksgiving carving out a spot for grindhouse connoisseurs on Hulu, and the transgressive Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma proving the genre can have brains and blood over on Mubi.
If you prefer your thrills giant-sized, look no further than Netflix, where the king of monsters can be seen stomping across Japan in the Academy Award–winning Godzilla Minus Zero.
Elsewhere, the Earth itself is in peril in a double bill of animated spectaculars. A warning from the future arrives in the stunning time-travel fantasy Arco, taking viewers on an imaginative journey across centuries on Hulu, while The Day the Earth Blew Up on HBO Max places Looney Tunes icons Daffy Duck and Porky Pig as the planet’s last line of defense. (We’re cooked.)
Here are WIRED’s picks of the best movies to watch right now.
Drawing inspiration from the works of Sylvain Chomet and Studio Ghibli in equal measure, director Ugo Bienvenu has created an absolutely gorgeous piece of animation. This French science fantasy epic follows 10-year-old Arco (Oscar Tresanini in French, Juliano Krue Valdi in English), who time-travels from his home in 2932 in hopes of seeing dinosaurs. Instead, he crashes in 2075, a point where humanity is on the brink of destruction, the planet wracked by brutal storms, its resources all but exhausted, and humanity living in protective bubbles.
Aided by schoolgirl Iris (Margot Ringard Oldra, Romy Fay) and her robot caretaker Mikki, Arco desperately tries to repair his damaged time-suit to return home. However, between environmental devastation, a strange trio hunting him, and his very presence risking the timeline, Arco’s time might be up. Beautiful but somber, Arco is one of the best yet sadly most overlooked films of the year, animated or otherwise.
What good is a kamikaze pilot who survives? That’s the question haunting Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki) at the end of WWII, outlasting both the conflict and an encounter with an impossible, dinosaur-like creature on an isolated island. Returning to a devastated Tokyo, the directionless, traumatized Kōichi forms a relationship with fellow survivor Noriko (Minami Hamabe), raising an orphaned baby together. Yet their ad hoc family life is put in the atomic-breath firing line of that strange monster he encountered years earlier, now mutated to colossal size by exposure to atomic tests and stomping angrily onto land. Without weapons, military, or even much of a functioning society, can a still-broken Japan possibly withstand the horror of Godzilla?
While Ichiro Honda’s original 1954 Godzilla was a towering reptilian metaphor for the unknown risks of unleashing nuclear weapons on the world, Godzilla Minus One sees director Takashi Yamazaki leap back almost a decade to explore themes of survivor’s guilt, national despair, and rebuilding community. It’s a kaiju movie with brains, but also a treat for the eyes; it won the Academy Award for Best Visual Effects. With sequel Godzilla Minus Zero in cinemas now, it’s well worth catching up on before seeing Big G throwing down with arch-nemesis King Ghidorah.
When struggling furniture seller Clark (Chiwetel Ejiofor) finds a crack in reality in his store’s basement, he becomes obsessed with exploring the seemingly infinite liminal space he’s slipped into. The space goes on forever, yet appears to be entirely empty—apart from an unseen presence stalking him. Becoming obsessed with mapping the unmappable, Clark’s already-fraying life disintegrates further, until his fixation ends up dragging his concerned therapist Mary (Renate Reinsve) into the Backrooms herself—except she doesn’t find it quite so uninhabited. And all the while, someone outside is watching closely.
From internet folklore to cinematic sensation, director Kane Parsons’ Backrooms was the surprise horror hit of the summer. It’s easy to see why—the endless sprawl of impossible corridors and uncanny rooms that connect in ways that seem to defy physics and geometry alike is darkly mesmerizing for viewers, while the unexplained nature of this twisted reality keeps you guessing at every turn. A sequel is in the works, but you can get lost in the Backrooms right now.
When up-and-coming director Kris (Hannah Einbinder) is hired to reboot the floundering Camp Miasma horror franchise, she wants to bring back Billy Presley (Gillian Anderson), the series’ original “Final Girl.” Unsettlingly, Kris finds Billy now living on the abandoned campsite from the dated first flick, living a reclusive life and obsessed with Little Death, the iconic killer from the series. Pitch meetings soon turn into the pair bonding over their fascination with, and experience of, the series—before descending into … well, the hint is in the film’s title.
A festival darling, picking up awards at both Cannes Film Festival and San Sebastián International Film Festival, this smart, transgressive horror outing from director Jane Schoenbrun ( We're All Going to the World's Fair, I Saw the TV Glow ) cleverly deconstructs the slasher genre and reexamines it from a queer—and extremely meta—perspective.
Somehow, despite a near-century of Looney Tunes cartoons (counting from 1930’s “ Sinkin’ in the Bathtub ”), The Day the Earth Blew Up is the series’ very first feature-length, fully animated movie (no, Space Jam doesn’t count). It’s been worth the wait, though—this loving pastiche of sci-fi B-movies is a stellar showcase for its top-billed stars, Daffy Duck and Porky Pig (both phenomenally voiced by the sadly departed Eric Bauza).
With an asteroid hurtling toward Earth, UFOs flying around, a sinister scientist meddling with unknown substances, and a zombie plague spread by infected bubble gum, Earth’s last hope is a deranged duck and an anxious pig. We’re probably doomed, but at least we’ll die laughing—this hilarious outing is a reminder of everything great about these beloved characters.
When Yu Kobayashi (Yuzu Aoki) transfers to a new school in rural Japan, he finds the strict culture and rigid conformity of students and staff alike unusual. Classes stand and bow to teachers in unnaturally uniform movements, PE lessons are precise marching practices, and even the hierarchy of bullies and victims seems oddly organized. Initially, Yu writes it off as culture clash in a new environment, until students inexplicably start to form ever-larger human pyramids, with teachers brutally encouraging them. Only Yu and outsider Ai Sato (Anna Yamada) seem able to resist the compulsion to join the pyramid—but with the increasingly maddening adherence to peer pressure spreading across Japan, they might be the only ones.
Director and writer Yûta Shimotsu expands the almost surreal setup into an exploration of conformity and expectations, infusing it all with an uncomfortable dose of J-horror. It’s exceedingly weird in places and demands you make your own conclusions, but at a brisk 81 minutes, it’s a short, sharp, and frequently shocking slice of satire.
Every holiday deserves a related slasher flick—everything from April Fools’ to Christmas to, of course, Halloween. Thanksgiving had been the odd one out, until 2007’s Grindhouse (the anthology double feature coheaded by Robert Rodriguez and Quentin Tarantino), which featured a bunch of mock trailers, including one by Hostel director Eli Roth, centered on a killer Pilgrim. Fast forward to 2023, and Roth finally got the idea out of his head with this full-length version.

The French Football Federation president, Philippe Diallo, has been confirmed as Uefa’s surprise late choice to run for the Fifa presidency. The search for a Uefa-backed candidate to challenge Gianni Infantino was taken to the wire, with Wednesday the deadline for those planning to contest the Fifa election in March.
“At a meeting held today and chaired by Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin, the national associations represented on the Uefa executive committee and the Fifa council invited Philippe Diallo, president of the French Football Federation (FFF), to stand as a candidate in the Fifa presidential election in March 2027 and unanimously pledged their full support,” a statement said.
Diallo emerged as the favourite after plans to enlist a decorated former player or manager did not reach fruition. Uefa said the 63‑year‑old had accepted the invitation and that his candidacy was due to be ratified on Tuesday by the FFF.
Diallo strongly criticised Infantino in September, saying: “His initiatives during and after the World Cup have seriously damaged the image and the unity of football. As a result, we believe that trust has been broken.”
It is unclear whether the move to back Diallo will spell the end of the campaign begun by Kozo Tashima , the honorary president of the Japanese Football Association, to challenge Infantino. Tashima, a Fifa council member, has influential backers within Uefa but its hierarchy appears to feel Diallo has a greater chance of wooing voters in other areas of the world.
In the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.
If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.
If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from the iOS App Store on iPhone or the Google Play store on Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.
Diallo is expected to win the backing of the vast majority of Uefa’s member associations and there are hopes he could pick up votes from Francophone members of the Confederation of African Football, which has been steadfast in its support for Infantino.
There are concerns that having multiple challengers to Infantino will strengthen his position and play into the hands of a campaign that will present the incumbent as the unity candidate after months of infighting.
Concacaf – the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation – has been reluctant to endorse an alternative candidate, despite opposing Infantino, with some federations arguing that a boycott of the election would send the strongest message regarding the need for governance reform.
Uefa’s decision to back Diallo represents a marked departure from its original approach, in which it sought to coalesce behind a more high‑profile figure who had made their name on the pitch or in the dugout. There had been late hope that Arsène Wenger, Fifa’s chief of global development, would put himself forward, but it would have required a major change of heart from him. Former players such as Mikaël Silvestre and, belatedly, Didier Drogba are understood to have expressed interest that never came to anything.
Diallo is a career administrator who has worked in French football since 1992, chairing the clubs’ lobby group Union des Clubs Professionnels de Football for almost 30 years before joining the FFF in 2021. He was elected president two years later in what was regarded in France as a shock victory, having initially stepped up in an interim capacity. Diallo in the same year joined Uefa’s executive committee.
Germany’s head coach, Jürgen Klopp , has said he would welcome a new president. “The general consensus is that a change might make sense. But what would interest me even more in this context, from a football perspective, is that we never thought things could get any worse after Sepp Blatter, and yet someone actually managed to make it worse.
“Right now, we’re thinking that if Mr Infantino were to leave, it would be cool if the next person could just do a better job. Because I believe it should be possible to do better.”

The US president oscillates between strike threats on Iran and insisting the war ‘militarily is effectively over’
A third US aircraft carrier has arrived in the Middle East, US Central Command said in a social media post on Monday, making a dramatic show of military might as Donald Trump keeps his options open for next steps in the Iran war.
The USS Theodore Roosevelt brings thousands of additional troops to the Middle East as Trump has oscillated between threatening additional large-scale strikes on Iran and insisting that the more than eight-month-old war “militarily is effectively over”.
The Roosevelt, along with its accompanying strike force, left San Diego in September. It joins the USS George HW Bush and the USS George Washington aircraft carriers, as well as smaller navy ships, which are in the region to maintain a naval blockade of Iranian shipping.
The George HW Bush arrived in the region in April, while the George Washington arrived in August. The navy previously had three carrier strike groups in the Middle East in April, for the first time since 2003.
In addition to the three aircraft carriers, the flotilla in the Arabian Sea now includes 13 destroyers, two cruisers and a littoral combat ship, according to the navy. Two more destroyers are in the Red Sea.
The Roosevelt had deployed along with the USS Makin Island amphibious readiness group, which includes the USS John P Murtha and USS Anchorage amphibious landing ships and around 2,000 marines. Those ships have yet to make it to the region.
The third carrier arrived nearly two weeks after midterm elections that saw voters deliver major losses to Trump’s Republican party, driven in part by the unpopularity of the Iran war and its economic effects. The results led JD Vance to publicly break with Trump over the conflict, posting on social media that “the reason we lost is the war”.
Trump has insisted it was the right thing to do and has not ruled out restarting the conflict, which has been locked in a stalemate for months.
Last week, Trump warned Iran that the US military is “locked and loaded” and that the US was keeping an eye on Pickaxe Mountain, a facility linked to Iran’s nuclear program, for signs of activity.
“If something does not work out, I would not hesitate” to act, Trump told conservative broadcaster Hugh Hewitt on Thursday.
Yet, Trump also told reporters last week that he believed it was highly unlikely he would need to order new major strikes on Iran, declaring that the war “militarily is effectively over” after meeting with Qatar’s prime minister.
Trump also declared that the US no longer needs a deal with Tehran and told Vance – who was a chief negotiator in earlier ceasefire talks – instead to focus on the administration’s domestic anti-fraud campaign targeting Democratic-controlled cities and states.
Negotiations have stalled due to differences over Iran’s nuclear program, an issue that Trump insists be part of any deal meant to end the war. Iran wants the US first to agree to several core conditions, including lifting the naval blockade that is stopping its oil from getting to world markets.
In the meantime, a focal point of the simmering conflict remains the strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway where a fifth of the world’s oil passed before the war.
Commercial ships are still coming under attack or facing other risks, while the US has carried out limited strikes on Iranian targets near the strait and is helping guide vessels through the contested waters.
Iranian state TV, quoting the naval arm of Iran’s revolutionary guard and the army, warned shipping companies Monday that a US-supported route through the waterway is dangerous because of mines.
Mines have damaged six oil tankers since Sunday, polluting the strait’s coastlines, according to the revolutionary guard’s navy.
Separately, a projectile struck a tanker trying to transit through the strait, starting an engine room fire, but no casualties were reported, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Organization said.
US Central Command, which oversees military operations in the Middle East, said it has redirected 150 merchant vessels and disabled five since June under the blockade.
Independent assessments from Lloyd’s List, a maritime tracking and analysis firm, show that traffic through the strait remains at less than a third of prewar levels.

The Kerch bridge was built in 2018 and is one of President Putin's signature infrastructure projects (file photo)
Russia says it has recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, in which a landmark bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea sustained minor damage and several oil refineries were hit.
The Russian military intercepted and destroyed 2,049 drones and four Flamingo long-distance missiles over 24 hours, officials said. Around 600 flew towards the capital alone, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin added.
Kyiv, meanwhile, came under a record 17 air raid alerts in a single day. At least seven people were killed by Russian strikes and attacks on energy infrastructure caused blackouts for 50,000 people.
The intense strikes come days after US, Ukrainian and Russian envoys held talks aimed at ending the war.
The war in Ukraine began with Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.
The Moscow-installed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, confirmed that drones had struck the Crimean Bridge connecting Russia with the annexed peninsula, leading to traffic restrictions.
The structure - also known as Kerch Bridge - was built by Russia after it invaded and annexed the peninsula in 2014. It was inaugurated by Russian President Vladimir Putin to great fanfare in 2018 and is carefully protected with multiple layers of aerial and maritime defences.
Russian pro-war military commentators said on Telegram that rather than a direct attack, the bridge had suffered from the impact of drone warhead debris. Neither Ukraine's domestic security service nor its main military intelligence directorate has responded to a BBC request for comment.
Atesh, a partisan Ukrainian group operating inside Russian-held territory, said on social media that authorities in Crimea were "bracing for further strikes" on the Kerch Bridge and that they felt Moscow did not appreciate the seriousness of the situation.
Ukrainian drones also hit several energy facilities, including an oil refinery in Ilsky, in the southern Krasnodar region, where falling drone debris sparked a fire and injured six people, including children.
Last week, President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Russia of carrying out a concerted operation against Ukraine's bridges in order to "divide Ukraine... and make life as difficult as possible for people" on both sides of the Dnipro River which cuts across the country.
Despite the high-level diplomacy and visits by US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff to both Putin and Zelensky, peace remains a distant prospect.
Moscow is uncompromising on its demands for Ukraine to cede territory and give up efforts to become a Nato member.
The Kremlin has now also started to talk again about the need to rethink Europe's "security architecture", often intended by Moscow to mean a scaled-down Nato presence in countries close to Russia.
The apparent willingness of the US to engage in this conversation has set off alarm bells among Ukraine's European partners, which are concerned their continent's security could be redrawn by Washington and Moscow without their involvement.
A team of six - Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Poland and a representative of the EU institutions - will represent Europe in future talks with Russia, Ukraine and the US.
But the Kremlin continues to be dismissive of European input.
"We have also said more than once we need to understand... how much their position will help the peace process," said spokesman Dmitri Peskov.
EU representatives kept pushing for "unconditional support" for Ukraine and "enhanced pressure" on Russia, Peskov said, adding that "this sort of wording rather suggests their reluctance to facilitate the peace process".

US President Donald Trump headed to Asia on Monday for economic talks and a planned trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on nuclear issues and the war in Ukraine. Trump also raised the possibility of meeting North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during his visit.
President Donald Trump was heading to Asia on Monday, turning his focus to economic deals and historic three-way nuclear talks with Russia and China as his administration adjusts to a new political reality in Washington. He said he may meet with Kim Jong Un while in China as the US looks to reengage North Korea on its nuclear program.
Trump also said he plans to talk about Russia’s nearly 5-year-old war in Ukraine during his highly anticipated meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian leader Vladimir Putin in China.
“We’ll talk about, my favorite subject, Ukraine. Ukraine’s losing Ukraine,” Trump told reporters at the White House on Monday morning before departing for Asia. “Russia is losing 25,000 soldiers in the month. So we’ll be talking about that.”
Trump suggested he’ll talk with the leaders about the war even after his administration officials on Friday told reporters that he would discuss nuclear disarmament and the Iran war with his Chinese and Russian counterparts but steer clear of Russia’s war with Ukraine.
Read more Xi, Trump and Putin to discuss 'world peace' at Shenzhen summit, China says
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky had expressed concern as Trump pushed for the meeting with Putin and Xi about the potential of the three leaders using the moment to redraw global spheres of influence.
Planning for the summit has drawn comparisons to the Yalta Conference, the 1945 gathering at which the leaders of the US, Britain and the Soviet Union agreed to divide Germany and Berlin into four military occupation zones and finalised plans for establishing the United Nations.
“We really don’t want this to turn into ‘Yalta 2, 3, 4’ with a redistribution of influence,” Zelenskyy said last month.
After hours of flying, Air Force One had been scheduled to stop in Anchorage, but instead headed to Fairbanks for an Alaska refueling stop. The change wasn’t announced until after the plane landed in Fairbanks and local media began posting pictures.
During the stop, an older model of Air Force One aircraft with the traditional baby blue paint scheme pulled up alongside the Qatari-gifted model, which Trump had been traveling on. There was no sign of Trump during the stop, or of any movement between the planes.
The newer presidential jet later took off, and the White House blamed the change on extreme weather conditions in Anchorage, saying Air Force One landed in Fairbanks in order to refuel in better climate conditions.
Read more Russia's war on Ukraine: 'Americans want to have a deal whatever the cost for both Ukraine & Europe'
Still, the alternative refueling location called to mind the July incident in Turkey when Trump secretly stowed away on a catering truck to fly out of the country after a NATO summit.
The White House made it appear then that the president was flying on Air Force One — and word of his secret swap didn't emerge until it was first reported by The Washington Post in August.
Trump’s departure follows the often-omnipresent president having remained largely out of public sight for the past several days, even as a nationwide ground stop snarled air traffic and his Republican administration faced tough questions on its handling of the situation.
Trump said he was kept up to date Friday about the ground stop by Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who held a briefing Friday evening to address the American public.
Trump defended his decision to delegate to the Cabinet officials to inform the public.
“I didn’t think there was any reason for me to do it," Trump said, adding, “I thought they did a very good job.”
His trip to Asia, which begins in Manila and then continues to the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen, gives him the opportunity to try to change the narrative from his domestic woes, including the air travel problems and fallout from the November midterm election where his party lost both chambers of Congress.
Read more It's 'game over' for Jensen Huang, king of AI chips
The controversy over tech powerhouse and chipmaker Nvidia is also certain to hang over Trump’s visit to China, despite efforts by administration officials to downplay the president’s close ties to Jensen Huang, who resigned as CEO last week after admitting to an affair with an alleged Chinese government agent.
Beijing has said it was not involved. Trump had no plans to raise the issue with Xi when the two leaders meet, said US officials who briefed reporters anonymously about the president’s Asia trip under ground rules set by the White House.
But the president came to Huang's defense, asserting he hasn't been told by officials that it's been determined that the executive from Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing and AI infrastructure provider whom Huang had an affair with, is in fact a Chinese agent. Trump added he'd like to see Huang reinstated as Nvidia's CEO.
“Well I don’t know that she’s a spy at all. Nobody’s proven that. He probably shouldn’t have been doing on a personal basis what he did," Trump said. “That’s a different story.”
Huang, who frequently speaks with Trump, accompanied the president on Air Force One during his last trip to China in May. Trump has argued that America needs to preserve its leadership on artificial intelligence, and warned of dire consequences if China wins that competition.
Scrutiny of the Trump administration’s actions as they relate to Nvidia has been growing, including on the Commerce Department’s delay in placing restrictions on Nvidia chip exports to Megaspeed.
Read more China to host first-ever trilateral meeting between Trump, Xi and Putin next week
Asked about the matter in an interview that aired Sunday with Fox News Channel anchor Larry Kudlow, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he will “leave the internal workings of the Commerce Department to the Commerce Department" but it was crucial “to examine whether Nvidia had a culture of compliance around the US export restrictions.”
Trump acknowledged tension between Treasury and Commerce on the matter. He suggested that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick may have delayed placing the export restrictions to avoid a “blow up” in the fragile US-China relationship.
“We’re having a very good relationship with China right now, and I understand both sides of it, and I’ll make a decision, but I understand very well both sides,” Trump said.
Regarding North Korea, Trump met with Kim on three occasions during his first term but has not been able to get him to meaningfully engage since his return to the White House. Trump has sought to set the groundwork for further talks with Kim. In August, he ordered the Pentagon to scale back joint military exercises with South Korea .
Trump, in an exchange with reporters before departing the White House for his flight for Manila, said Kim “may come” to Shenzhen but “that's up to President Xi.”
Among the travelers on the Asia trip with Trump will be Elon Musk , the head of SpaceX and Tesla , who is shaping up to be a top investigative target of the incoming Democratic majority in Congress.
In the Philippines , Trump will meet with Southeast Asian leaders who look to the United States for help countering Beijing’s aggression in the region. He plans to sign a trade deal with Thailand while in Manila, the White House said.
Then he heads to China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit — and at the end of the trip, the first-ever three-way talks with China's Xi and Russia's Putin to discuss nuclear stockpiles.

Almanya dahil 5 Avrupa ülkesi, iltica başvurusu reddedilen düzensiz göçmenleri 2027'den itibaren Ruanda'da kurulacak "geri gönderme merkezine" sınır dışı etmeyi planlıyor. İnsan hakları kuruluşları tepkili.
Avrupa Birliği (AB) üyesi beş ülke, sığınma başvuruları reddedilen kişileri önümüzdeki yıl itibariyle Afrika ülkesi Ruanda'da kurulacak " geri gönderme merkezine " sınır dışı etmek için hazırlık yapıldığını duyurdu.
Açıklama, Viyana'da bugün Almanya, Avusturya, Danimarka, Hollanda ve Yunanistan hükümetlerinin, Ruanda İçişleri Bakanı Vincent Biruta ile gerçekleştirdikleri toplantının ardından yapıldı.
Toplantıya ev sahipliği yapan Avusturya'nın Başbakanı Christian Stocker, Ruanda ile ilk geri gönderme merkezinin 2027'de faaliyete geçmesi için yürütülen müzakerelerde ilerleme sağlandığını söyledi.
Danimarka Başbakanı Mette Frederiksen ise "dönüm noktası" olarak nitelendirdiği girişim için, "Bunun, yasa dışı göçün yarattığı büyük zorluklarla mücadele etmemizi sağlayacak, oyunun kurallarını değiştiren bir adım olacağını düşünüyorum" dedi.
Frederiksen, diğer birçok Avrupa ülkesinin de bu girişime katılacağını ve bu yolla "insan kaçakçılarının iş modelini, düzensiz göçü teşvik eden unsurları ortadan kaldıracaklarını" öne sürdü.
Avrupa ülkeleri, Ruanda ile önümüzdeki birkaç ay içinde müzakereleri tamamlayarak nihai anlaşmayı imzalamayı hedefliyor.
AB üyesi beş ülke, bu sayede iltica talepleri reddedilenlerin hızlıca Avrupa'dan Afrika'ya sınır dışı edilmesini sağlamayı amaçlıyor.
Ayrıca Afrika'ya sınır dışı edilme riskinin, Avrupa'ya gelmeye niyetlenen düzensiz göçmenler açısından da caydırıcı olması umut ediliyor.
Friedrich Merz başbakanlığındaki Alman hükümetinin Hristiyan Sosyal Birlik (CSU) partili (CSU), Ruanda girişimini "yenilikçi bir çözüm" sözleriye övdü.
Düzensiz göçmenlerin geldikleri ülkelere sınır dışı edilmelerinde zorluklarla karşılaşıldığını ifade eden Dobrindt, böyle bir çözüm imkanına ihtiyaç duyulduğunu savundu.
Bakan Dobrindt, mevcut planın, İngiltere'nin Ruanda ile yaptığı ve sonunda başarısızlığa uğrayan anlaşmadan farklı olduğunu da savundu.
Dobrindt, İngiltere'nin sığınma işlemlerini Ruanda'ya taşımak istediğini, kendilerinin ise bir Avrupa ülkesinde sığınma başvurusu reddedilen ve bulunduğu ülkeyi terk etmekle yükümlü olan kişileri Ruanda'ya göndereceklerini kaydetti.
Ruanda İçişleri Bakanı Vincent Biruta, ülkesinin Avrupa'da kalma hakkı bulunmayan kişilere "ikinci bir şans" vereceğini söyledi.
Biruta, ülkesine sınır dışı edilecek kişilere "gönüllü olarak menşe ülkelerine dönme, Ruanda toplumuna entegre olma veya yasal olarak ikamet etme hakkına sahip oldukları başka bir yere yerleşme fırsatı sunulacağını" belirtti.
Bakan Biruta'ya, Ruanda'nın mültecilerin insan haklarını nasıl güvence altına alacağı sorusu yöneltildi. Ülkesinin Birleşmiş Milletler Mülteciler Yüksek Komiserliği (UNHCR) gibi kuruluşları sürece dahil edeceğini belirten Vincent Biruta, "bağımsız bir izleme mekanizması" inşa edileceğini de kaydetti.
İnsan hakları örgütleri ise Avrupalı ülkelerin göçmenlerin haklarına üçüncü ülkelerde saygı gösterileceğini garanti edemeyeceğini savunarak, kişilerin bu ülkelerdeki merkezlere gönderilmesi planlarını eleştiriyor.
İnsan Hakları İzleme Örgütü'nden Clementine de Montjoye yaptığı açıklamada, "Avrupa dışında kurulan sınır dışı merkezleri, AB'nin sorumluluklarını başka ülkelere devretme çabasının en yeni ve alaycı tezahürüdür" diyerek tepki gösterdi.
Montjoye, "Kigali'ye bir sınır dışı programına ev sahipliği yapması için ödeme yapmak, yalnızca sınır dışı edilenlerin acı çekmesine ve zarar görmesine yol açmakla kalmaz, aynı zamanda ülke içinde ve dışında ciddi insan hakları ihlallerinden sorumlu bir hükümete finansman ve siyasi nüfuz sağlar" diye konuştu.
Uluslararası Af Örgütü Almanya'nın Genel Sekreteri Julia Duchrow da "İnsanları hiçbir bağlarının olmadığı ve haklarının korunmasının güvence altında bulunmadığı üçüncü ülkelere sınır dışı etmek yalnızca insanlık dışı değildir. Bu aynı zamanda siyasi açıdan ileri görüşlülükten yoksundur ve insan hakları bakımından son derece büyük riskler taşır" açıklamasını yaptı.
Uluslararası Af Örgütünün Avusturya'daki sığınma ve göç uzmanı Aimée Stuflesser de girişimi "büyük bir utanç" olarak nitelendirerek, "İnsanları daha önce hiç bulunmadıkları bir ülkeye göndermek sorumsuzluktur. Ruanda anlaşmasının, denetim imkanlarının sınırlı olması nedeniyle insan hakları açısından acımasız bir kara deliğe dönüşmesi yönünde gerçek bir tehlike vardır" uyarısını yaptı.
Uluslararası Af Örgütü, Ruanda’da yargı bağımsızlığının ciddi biçimde kısıtlanmış olduğuna, insanların bazen aylar boyunca, çoğu zaman haklarında suçlama yöneltilmeden cezaevinde tutulduğuna dikkat çekiyor.
Ruanda'nın AB ve ABD'nin yaptırım uyguladığı bir ülke olduğuna, Almanya'nın bu devletle yürüttüğü ikili kalkınma iş birliğini de askıya aldığına işaret ediliyor.

What happens next in Yemen may send fresh shockwaves to the world economy
The Iran-backed Houthi rebels who seized much of Yemen in 2014 have now forced the army of the internationally recognised government to withdraw from the Red Sea coast in order to defend their interim capital, Aden.
Their advance bodes ill for Yemen's legitimate, internationally recognised government, its Saudi backers and, by extension, much of the rest of the world.
Yemen, a mountainous, heavily armed, intensely tribal and largely impoverished nation, sits at the far south-west corner of the Arabian Peninsula.
The country has two coasts: One faces the Indian Ocean on which sits the once-prosperous trading port of Aden, the other faces the Red Sea and, most importantly, the narrow chokepoint at the southern exit of that waterway - the so-called Bab al-Mandab Strait or, in English, The Gate of Tears.
Whoever controls that strait can threaten any or all maritime traffic passing through from both the Mediterranean and the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean.
In normal times, it accounts for around 12% of global trade, with anywhere between 70 to 150 ships a day making the transit.
But not any more. Although the Houthis say they are no threat to maritime traffic, they are currently at war with Saudi Arabia, making it extremely hazardous for the Saudis to send their oil tankers past the now rebel-controlled coast.
When the US and Israel started a war with Iran in February, Tehran responded by choking off much of the oil trade flowing out of the Gulf through another narrow chokepoint - the Strait of Hormuz. This sent oil prices soaring, boosted inflation and hurt economies everywhere.
The Saudis had a Plan B. Instead of exporting their oil past the dangerous coast of Iran, where their tankers risked being droned or mined by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, they started pumping it overland through their East-West Pipeline to an export terminal on the Red Sea at Yanbu. This worked for a while.
But then in July a cold truce between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis broke down, that pipeline got hit by drones and the rebels started firing missiles and drones at targets all over Saudi Arabia.
On land, the Houthis seized the initiative and made a lightning dash down the Red Sea coast, sending the Yemeni army into headlong retreat. A brief counter-offensive appears to have failed and the Houthis are now reported to be in full control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait and the nearby offshore islands.
Nicholas Hopton, a former British Ambassador to both Yemen and Iran and now director-general of the UK-based Middle East Association, says: "The decision by the legitimate government of Yemen to prioritise the military defence of Aden at the expense of withdrawing from other areas suggests that the war is not going well for the Saudi-backed [Yemeni] government. And the rest of the world should be worried."
He warns that if the port of Aden – a city of roughly 1.25 million inhabitants – was to fall to the Houthis, it "would undoubtedly precipitate a further escalation in the regional crisis and further fragility in the global economy, catalysed by the US-Iran war".
But Mohammed al-Basha, the Yemeni founder of the US-based risk advisory firm Basha Report, believes the Houthis would struggle to capture the heavily fortified city of Aden.
"Any attempt to seize a densely populated city like Aden would come at a significant human cost," Basha said. "Advancing across the flat coastal plains would also expose Houthi forces to air power."
"For now, the Houthis appear to be seeking a negotiated surrender, hoping to exploit infighting and divisions among southern factions to achieve their objectives without a costly urban offensive."
It is conceivable that the Yemen war will settle into a less dramatic but deeply unsatisfactory stasis - a situation where casualty figures subside yet the country remains split between areas controlled by the Houthis - Iran's Shia allies - and the disparate and often poorly motivated forces of the Saudi-backed Yemeni army.
The former British defence attaché to Yemen, Col Iain Smailes, warned that the recent Houthi advance could trigger a spike in oil prices, as it did when they seized the Bab al-Mandab Strait in September.
He also warns this could have a knock-on effect to security well beyond Yemen's borders.
"By extending their control over the western coastline, the Houthis will increase their ability to smuggle weapons and ammunition from Iran, the Horn of Africa and elsewhere, posing additional threats to the region," Col Smailes said.
"This control will enable both Iran and the Houthis to extend their influence in East Africa and beyond."

Ukraine has held new talks with United States and European officials on ending the war with Russia, hours before Kyiv’s mayor reported strikes on two bridges in the capital.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described Monday’s online discussions with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and European representatives as “not easy”. But he said participants had agreed to meet in Berlin with the “Coalition of the Willing”, a group of countries supporting Ukraine, as the US and Europe step up peace talks this week.
“Diplomatic processes are actively underway and we hope that these efforts will not be in vain,” Zelenskyy said in his nightly address.
He also warned that Ukrainian intelligence indicated Russia was preparing major strikes that night and throughout Tuesday.
Later on Monday, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said preliminary reports indicated that the North and South bridges across the Dnipro River had been hit. Air defence units were operating, and Reuters news agency witnesses heard a series of loud explosions.
Ukraine on Monday struck a key bridge and targeted oil refineries in what Russian defence ministry data indicated was the biggest overnight drone attack on Russia since the start of full-scale war in 2022. The Crimea Bridge was again struck overnight, with nearly 200 drones intercepted near Moscow, according to Telegram statements.
Kushner, US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, said Washington was making progress towards an agreement in coordination with Russia, Ukraine and Europe.
“Important challenges remain, and a final agreement will require difficult decisions,” he wrote on X.
He said he and Witkoff had also spoken with Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov about the next steps. Their discussions included how to arrange direct engagement between Europe and Russia so each could hear the other’s concerns and proposals.
The exchanges followed last week’s talks in Abu Dhabi , where US, Ukrainian and Russian officials met together for the first time in nine months. Those negotiations produced an agreement on a prisoner exchange but no breakthrough on ending the war.
Witkoff and Kushner later met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow and said European representatives would join the next round. On Monday, Moscow disputed that assertion.
Zelenskyy said representatives from France, Germany, Britain, Italy and Poland had participated fully in Monday’s discussion and would have the same representation in future meetings with Russian negotiators.
Ushakov said Russia had not agreed to expand the talks beyond the existing Russian, Ukrainian and US delegations. No date had been agreed for the next round, he added.
European governments, meanwhile, were preparing their negotiating team while maintaining pressure on Moscow.
Irish Foreign Minister Helen McEntee welcomed renewed talks and the agreement on EU representation following diplomatic meetings in Abu Dhabi and Dublin last week. But she said, “Russia has clearly not changed its position.”
Speaking ahead of Monday’s meeting of EU foreign ministers in Brussels, McEntee said 113 new sanctions on Russia were intended to maintain pressure on Moscow “as it intensified attacks on civilians and critical infrastructure during the winter”.
“We are also working to ensure Ukraine has the finance and the military support it needs while advancing Ukraine’s path to EU membership,” she said.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Russia wanted a lasting peace rather than a temporary ceasefire that would allow Ukraine to recover from the damage inflicted by Russian forces.
He said Moscow sought peace lasting “years, even centuries”, adding that negotiations were complex and could take considerable time.
Separately, Trump said he would discuss the war with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Putin in China, saying he believed Putin wanted to end the war.
“I think he’s backing down a little bit,” Trump told reporters. “Frankly, I think he’d like to see it finish.”
The planned Berlin meeting would allow Ukraine and its supporters to agree on their next negotiating steps. Russia had yet to accept their proposed representation in the talks that would follow.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham says UK lost more than it gained after its divorce from the bloc.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the Brexit promise failed to deliver for the United Kingdom and that the country needs to reset its relationship with the European Union to combat growing global isolationism.
During a speech at the Lord Mayor’s Banquet in London on Monday, Burnham compared the outcome of Britain’s divorce from the EU, triggered by a 2016 referendum, to the Hans Christian Andersen fairy tale “The Emperor’s New Clothes”, in which no one is willing to tell the ruler that he is, in fact, naked.
“I do try to say things as I see them,” Burnham said. “And to be frank, we have lost more than we have gained in the last 10 years. The hard Brexit we were given is not good enough for Britain.”
The remarks come ahead of a UK-EU summit in Brussels on Friday, which Burnham said could deliver “real improvements in people’s everyday lives in areas of the country that have felt neglected for too long”.
Any deal, he said, would have to pass three tests: it would have to be consistent with Labour’s manifesto and red lines, improve the Brexit deal to align with what people voted for in 2016 and pass his Makerfield Test, his benchmark for ensuring real improvements for people in parts of the UK that have long felt neglected.
The meeting is a key step in his pledge to reset relations with the 27-nation bloc a decade after the UK voted to leave and six years after its 2020 departure.
The UK is expected to seal a deal on trading food and drink, and make agreements on energy and emissions and a plan to let young people work for limited periods across Britain and the EU.
Burnham said the promise of the pro-Brexit campaign that Britain would “take back control” of its borders, laws and economy had not been delivered. Trade with EU countries has dropped sharply, and estimates of the economic damage range from 4 percent to 8 percent of the UK’s gross domestic product, he said.
Seeking to draw a line under a decade of political turmoil that has made him Britain’s seventh prime minister since 2016, Burnham said the UK was back on the world stage. He argued the country is well positioned to lead in an era of renewed international cooperation because of its experience since 2016.
“Brexit was the first domino to fall in a global move towards more isolationism and protectionism,” he said. “It is exactly what our enemies wanted. Russia wanted disunity within NATO and a weaker Europe.”
Burnham said that he will open a discussion with EU partners on Britain’s long-term relationship with the bloc soon after the Brussels summit. His spokesperson Tom Wells said on Monday that “no assumptions are being made” and “the British public will be the boss of any outcome”.
Until the next national election, Burnham remains bound by the pledge of Keir Starmer, whom he replaced as centre-left Labour Party leader and prime minister, not to rejoin the bloc’s tariff-free customs union or frictionless single market for goods, services and workers.
Erasing that pledge would reignite a subject that split the country: the 2016 referendum vote was 52 percent in favour of leaving the EU and 48 percent in support of remaining.

Kızılcık Şerbeti 'nden ayrılığı aylar sonra yeniden konuşulmaya başlanan Sibel Taşçıoğlu'nun yalanlamasının ardından bu kez Feyza Civelek'ten açıklama geldi. Dizinin Nilay'ı olarak tanınan oyuncu, sosyal medyada kendisini hedef alan iddiaların bütünüyle gerçek dışı olduğunu söyledi. Civelek, avukatı aracılığıyla yasal sürecin başlatıldığını da duyurdu.
Kızılcık Şerbeti 'nde Pembe karakterine üç sezon hayat veren Sibel Taşçıoğlu, birkaç gündür sosyal medyada kendi adıyla dolaşan ifadelerin kendisine ait olmadığını açıklamıştı. Oyuncu, yazılı açıklamasında 'Böyle bir açıklamam ya da röportajım olmamıştır' demişti.
Taşçıoğlu aynı paylaşımda, başka bir oyuncuyu küçük düşüren, kişisel ve mahrem konular üzerinden üretilen iddiaların kendi adı kullanılarak yayılmasını 'son derece yanlış' bulduğunu vurgulamıştı. 'Hiç kimsenin itibarlarının bu şekilde zedelenmesini doğru bulmadım, bugün de bulmuyorum' sözleri sosyal medyada kısa sürede gündem olmuştu.
Kızılcık Şerbeti'nden çıkarılan Sibel Taşçıoğlu'nun diziden gitme sebebinin Feyza Civelek olduğu iddia edilmiş ve söz konusu iddia uzun süre sosyal medyada yer almıştı.
Taşçıoğlu'nun ardından sessizliğini bozan isim Feyza Civelek oldu. Yeni dizisinin çekimleri başlamadan önce Marakeş'te tatil yapan oyuncu, yazılı bir açıklama yayımlayarak son günlerde adını hedef alan paylaşımlara yanıt verdi.
Civelek, çeşitli sosyal medya hesaplarında 'sistematik bir şekilde yürütülen karalama kampanyasının artarak sürdürüldüğüne' tanık olduğunu söyledi. Kişilik haklarını ve meslek hayatını hedef alan iddiaları 'onur kırıcı' ve 'mesleki itibarını zedelemeye yönelik' sözleriyle nitelendiren oyuncu, bunların tamamen asılsız olduğunu vurguladı.
Açıklamanın en dikkat çekici kısmı ise atılacak hukuki adımlar oldu. Civelek, iddiaları üretenler ve yayanlar hakkında avukatı Ümit Abanoz tarafından yasal işlemlere başlandığını duyurdu.
Oyuncu, suç duyurusunda bulunulacağını, manevi tazminat davası açılacağını ve tüm yasal haklarını kullanacağını da kamuoyuyla paylaştı. Üstelik süreç yalnızca iddiaları ortaya atan hesapları değil, bu paylaşımları yayanları da kapsıyor.

Fatih Terim’in 83 bin TL’lik restoran hesabını imzalı Galatasaray formalarıyla kapattığı iddiası sosyal medyada hızla yayılmıştı. Restoranın sahibi şef Fatih Tutak, iddiaların gerçeği yansıtmadığını söyledi. Tutak’a göre hesap eksiksiz ödendi. Üstelik imzalanan forma sayısı da konuşulandan çok daha fazlaydı.
Geçtiğimiz günlerde sosyal medyada dikkat çekici bir iddia dolaşmaya başladı. Buna göre Fatih Terim, İstanbul Bomonti'deki bir restoranda yediği akşam yemeğinin ardından önüne gelen 83 bin TL'lik hesabı parayla değil, üç imzalı Galatasaray formasıyla kapatmıştı.
Alışılmadık ödeme iddiası kısa sürede sosyal medyanın gündemine otururken iddiaya konu restoranın, Michelin yıldızlı şef Fatih Tutak'a ait olduğu da kısa sürede öğrenildi.
Günaydın yazarı Bülent Cankurt, iddianın doğru olup olmadığını öğrenmek için doğrudan restoranın sahibi Fatih Tutak'ı aradı. Tutak'ın anlattıkları ise sosyal medyada konuşulanlarla hiç örtüşmedi. Ünlü şefe göre Fatih Terim restorana kızı Buse Terim'le birlikte geldi ve 14 aşamalı tadım menüsünü tercih etti.
Tadım menüsü, şefin mutfağını baştan sona tanımak isteyen konukların seçtiği, çok sayıda küçük tabaktan oluşan uzun bir akşam yemeği deneyimi sunuyor. Akşamın sonunda hesap da eksiksiz şekilde ödendi. Yani formaların hesabın karşılığı olarak verildiği iddiası gerçeği yansıtmıyordu.
Peki iddianın çıkış noktası olan formalar ne oldu? Tutak, Terim'in o akşam gerçekten forma imzaladığını doğruladı. Ancak ortada konuşulduğu gibi üç değil, tam 20 imzalı forma vardı.
Tutak'ın açıklamasıyla birlikte formaların hesapla hiçbir ilgisi olmadığı da anlaşıldı. Hesap, formalardan bağımsız olarak eksiksiz ödenmişti.
Ünlü şef, keyifli geçen bir akşamın bu şekilde yansıtılmasından duyduğu üzüntüyü de gizlemedi. Tutak, 'Koskoca Fatih Terim'in böyle bir şeye ihtiyacı olabileceğini nasıl düşünür insanlar' sözleriyle tepkisini dile getirdi.
Tutak'a göre asıl üzücü olan, güzel bir anının bambaşka bir hikâyeye dönüşmesiydi. Şef, 'Bu kadar mutlu ve güzel bir anıyı bu şekilde algılamaları çok onur kırıcı' dedi.

ABD merkezli yatırım bankası JPMorgan, Türkiye ekonomisine yönelik değerlendirmelerinde 2027'de geçerli olacak yeni asgari ücret artışına odaklandı. Daha önce asgari ücreti doğru tahmin eden dev banka, 2027 asgari ücret için zam oranını verdi.
Aralık ayında başlayacak asgari ücret tespit süreci yaklaşırken, uluslararası finans kuruluşlarının Türkiye raporları piyasalarda yakından takip ediliyor. Geçmiş dönemlerdeki isabetli enflasyon ve ücret öngörüleriyle dikkat çeken ABD 'li bankacılık devi JPMorgan, temmuz ayında yayımladığı Türkiye analizinde ücret artışlarının makroekonomik dengeler üzerindeki etkisini masaya yatırdı.
JPMorgan analizinde, Aralık 2026'da asgari ücrete yapılacak artış oranının yalnızca çalışanların alım gücü açısından değil, 2027 yılında izlenecek para politikalarının yönünü anlamak bakımından da belirleyici olacağı vurgulandı.
Analizde, ücret artışının yüzde 30 veya bu oranın üzerinde gerçekleşmesi durumunda, seçim takvimi ve seçim öncesinde devreye alınacak ekonomi politikaları için önemli bir gösterge niteliği taşıyacağına işaret edildi.
Raporda öne çıkan en dikkat çekici başlıklardan biri de mevcut ücretlerin yaşam maliyetleri karşısındaki durumu oldu. JPMorgan, 2026 yılı sonuna gelindiğinde asgari ücret ile açlık sınırı arasındaki farkın yüzde 35'e ulaşmasını bekliyor. Banka analistleri, aralık ayındaki zam oranının bu farkın ne ölçüde telafi edileceğiyle doğrudan bağlantılı olarak ele alındığını ifade etti.

İspanya hükümeti, 2027'den itibaren asgari ücreti yüzde 5,3 artırarak aylık 1.286 euroya çıkarmayı planlıyor. Çalışma Bakanı Yolanda Diaz 'ın Pazartesi günü duyurduğu zam, sosyalistlerin öncülüğündeki hükümetin 2018'de göreve gelmesinden bu yana dokuzuncu asgari ücret artışı olacak.
Açıklama, 29 Kasım'da yapılacak genel seçime iki haftadan kısa bir süre kala geldi. Sosyalistler ve radikal sol müttefikleri, kamuoyu yoklamalarının çoğunda muhalefetin gerisinde yer alıyor.
Planlanan zam oranı, İspanya Merkez Bankası'nın bu yıl için öngördüğü yüzde 3,9'luk enflasyonun ve Ekim itibarıyla son 12 ayda kaydedilen yüzde 4,9'luk enflasyonun üzerinde bulunuyor.
Düzenlemeyle aylık asgari ücret 65 euro (71,64 dolar) artacak. İspanya'da asgari ücret, Temmuz ve Aralık aylarında verilen iki ek maaş dahil yılda 14 taksitte ödeniyor.
Hükümete göre, vergiden muaf tutulacak artıştan çoğunluğunu kadınların ve gençlerin oluşturduğu 2,5 milyondan fazla çalışan yararlanacak. Diaz yaptığı açıklamada, artışın Salı günkü Bakanlar Kurulu toplantısında onaylanacağını söyledi.
Planlanan zamla birlikte İspanya'da asgari ücret, 2018'e göre yaklaşık yüzde 75 artmış olacak. Bu artış, dokuz yılda aylık 550 euroya karşılık geliyor.

Radio 4 presenter Emma Barnett is set to leave the Today programme this week for a multiplatform new BBC show in the New Year.
Former Woman's Hour host Barnett has developed a "bold" new show, she says, which will launch in 2027 across BBC Sounds, BBC iPlayer and YouTube.
Her final day presenting Radio 4's flagship morning news and current affairs show will be on Wednesday 18 November.
"For the last nearly six years - it's been incredible to talk to the mighty Radio 4 listeners," she said in a statement. "Having proudly hosted Woman's Hour and now the Today Programme - I've had the rare pleasure of hosting nearly every hour of the morning on this truly unique and special radio network."
She added: "But it's not goodbye to the BBC audience I value so greatly because I have something else for them that I hope will add something meaningful and entertaining to their lives."
Posting on Instagram , external , she said there would be more information on what her new show would be about soon.
Barnett joined Today in May 2024, taking over from Martha Kearney to work alongside co-presenters Nick Robinson, Mishal Husain, Amol Rajan and Justin Webb. Husain and Rajan have since left.
Today programme editor Rebecca Keating said Barnett had brought "enormous energy" to Today, with "a keen focus" on listeners.
She noted how Barnett had a proven "track record of telling stories of personal hardship that influence public debate" but how she was "also equally at home interviewing British icons like Dame Judi Dench.
"We will miss her generous tea making and wish her every success in her new venture."
In August, Barnett, 41, revealed she had had a hysterectomy and surgery for endometriosis, days before a documentary she made about the condition was broadcast.
She returned to the Today programme explaining she had been absent in recent weeks because she was in hospital "in a case of life imitating work".
Speaking on her BBC podcast, Ready to Talk with Emma Barnett, last year, she told listeners that finding out she was going through perimenopause at the age of 38 felt like she had been "mugged, robbed".
The broadcaster said it was the "first time in my life I haven't really wanted to be a woman - it's the first time I've thought, I'd really quite like to be a bloke".
Radio 4 controller Mohit Bakaya said he was "delighted she's staying with the BBC" and would "look forward to her new show."

Portekiz'de katıldığı bir törende açıklamalarda bulunan Dolores Aveiro, oğlunun kandırıldığını ve milli takımda değerinin bilinmediğini savunurken, veda töreninin Ronaldo sahadayken yapılması gerektiğini dile getirdi.

Sir Tom Jones cancelled or rescheduled four dates on the US-leg of his tour last month due to illness
Sir Tom Jones has announced two headline shows in Wales just weeks after he was forced to cancel or reschedule a number of tour dates due to illness.
The 86-year-old Welsh music icon's homecoming, as part of his Come Gather Round world tour, will see him perform at Cardiff Castle on 30 May, followed by a fully-seated show at Llangollen Pavilion in Denbighshire on 28 June.
Heather Small will feature as a special guest at the Cardiff show, while soul band Stone Foundation will also join the bill at both concerts.
It is a return to home soil for the legendary singer from Pontypridd, Rhondda Cynon Taf, who last performed in Wales in summer 2025.
Last month, Sir Tom was forced to cancel or reschedule shows in the US-leg of the world tour, due to "a bad case of flu".
He said at the time that he was "truly sorry" for the disappointment caused to fans, later adding he feared his life was "over" after being admitted to hospital.
Tickets for his Welsh gigs go on sale on 20 November, and the sets will feature tracks from his 2021 album Surrounded By Time, alongside fan favourites including It's Not Unusual, What's New Pussycat?, Delilah and Green, Green Grass of Home.
Nick Saunders, founder of promoter Depot Live, said: "Tom Jones is a true Welsh icon, so it's a real pleasure to welcome him back to Cardiff Castle.
"He's one of Wales' greatest-ever musical exports, and there's always a real sense of pride in seeing him perform on home soil."
Dave Danford, artistic director of the Llangollen International Musical Eisteddfod, added: "His show here in 2024 was one of the most memorable evenings in the venue's history, and we've been trying to find a way to get him back here ever since."

The Last Week Tonight host memorialized the performative cruelty of Trump’s short-lived immigration prison in the Florida Everglades
J ohn Oliver opened the season finale of Last Week Tonight with a brief reaction to the Federal Aviation Administration’s shock grounding of all US flights on Friday afternoon, which brought nationwide travel to a halt and stranded travelers across the country. He zoned in on transportation secretary Sean Duffy, whose Friday press conference in the midst of a crisis left much to be desired. “Rather than use that press conference to dispense information, which would have been ideal, he instead took it as an opportunity to air grievances and make demands,” Oliver noted.
Duffy blamed “old, legacy equipment that failed” and asked for $50bn from Congress to upgrade the system. “I can’t build things if i don’t have money,” Duffy said. “I want $50bn. President Trump is a builder. He is going to build this network for the American people.”
“What are you doing going on TV to demand $50bn?” Oliver mocked. “You sound less like a secretary of transportation trying to calm people down and more like a Batman villain trying to hold Gotham hostage: ‘I need $50bn unless the Batman can solve my riddles in time!’”
Duffy, said Oliver, was right about one thing: the US flight system is outdated. But as the host pointed out, Republicans have controlled both houses of Congress as well as the presidency for the past two years, making them responsible for any complaints about underfunding. And the Republican-led Congress, along with the Trump administration, collaborated to triple Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)’s budget last year to $28bn, for a total that surpasses the annual budgets of almost all federal law enforcement agencies combined.
“It is hard to take a panicked shakedown from Duffy,” said Oliver, “not just because his cost estimate jumped by $20bn mid-sentence, but also because he’s part of a flagrantly corrupt administration who spent a chunk of his time in office shooting a shitty reality show with his family to encourage Americans to take more road trips.” (Duffy, his wife and their nine kids shot The Great American Road Trip over seven months from 2025 to 2026.)
“To that end,” said Oliver in reference to reports of stranded travelers renting cars last minute, “guess what, Sean? Mission fucking accomplished!”
In his main segment, Oliver tracked the rise and fall of “Alligator Alcatraz”, the prison opened last year in the Florida Everglades by the state’s then governor, Ron DeSantis, to curry favor with immigration hardliners like Trump.
“You might understandably have forgotten about Alligator Alcatraz given, you know, everything else,” said Oliver. “And this is the rare story where I’m actually going to tell you up front how it ends, and an even rarer one, given that it’s actually good news.” Because back in June, the Florida governor, Ron DeSantis, announced that the prison was closing down immediately. “And that is a genuinely good thing,” said Oliver. “Which is almost hard to absorb, isn’t it? The last few years, whenever you hear something was shut down, you naturally assume it’s an important clinical trial, or critical repairs at national parks, or maybe a beloved celebrity’s heart, not actually something you want to see end.”
But though it’s now closed, Oliver argued that the erstwhile prison is still worth talking about. “For one thing, Alligator Alcatraz is a pretty good encapsulation of the performative cruelty of Trump’s second term,” he said. “But also, one of the key men behind it, Ron DeSantis, is now being floated as a possible replacement for Pete Hegseth, and there’s even rumors that he’s planning another White House run.”
“And I am sure that DeSantis, like many of those who were behind Alligator Alcatraz, would like nothing more than for people to forget about it and move on. But … that should not happen.”
The host then retraced the prison’s “incredibly stupid origins” as a “mashup of two different ill-thought-through ideas that Trump floated”. One was his first-term interest in a border wall with a water-filled trench stocked with snakes and/or alligators. Another was his proposal to reopen Alcatraz, the infamous island prison located within the San Francisco Bay. Florida attorney general James Uthmeier, one of many “mid-tier villains in Trump’s orbit”, appears to have smushed together the two slapdash ideas into a proposal pitched via social media, claiming such a prison would be “efficient and low cost” because one doesn’t have to invest too much in a “perimeter”.
Trump’s team loved the idea, and the facility was assembled in under eight days – “slower than God, sure, but a lot faster than most high-intensity builds”, Oliver noted. To do so, the Florida state government relied on no-bid emergency contracts, including $219m to a portable restrooms company called Doodie Calls. In all, Alligator Alcatraz cost more than $1bn to construct, by using funds set aside for hurricanes, floods and other natural disasters because DeSantis declared US immigration in Florida to be a “state of emergency”. The vast majority of people incarcerated there, it should be noted, were neither convicted of a violent crime nor on a “final removal” order.
Perhaps unsurprisingly for a swamp prison, conditions were reportedly terrible – cramped and unsanitary, with open toilets, rotten food and literal cages branded as “calming areas” for men to “reflect on their behavior choices, manage their emotions, reduce stress and practice self-directed behavior”.
Though one would think inhumane practices would close the prison, what actually shut Alligator Alcatraz down “wasn’t everyone suddenly having an attack of conscience”, said Oliver: “Instead, it seems to have been a very stupid oversight on Ron DeSantis’s part.” The governor had said that the costs of the prison would be fully reimbursed by the federal government, but the federal government legally had to declare it a state project, sticking Florida with all of the costs.
The passing of the buck is one of many, many reasons, Oliver argued, states should not be allowed to run immigration detention facilities, full stop. “I’d actually argue that we shouldn’t be running immigration detention facilities in general, but that is a different story that we have already done,” he added.
Even though Alligator Alcatraz is no more, “we should remember the utter disgrace that it was”, he concluded. Ultimately, Alligator Alcatraz was “a shoddy, shameless attempt to gain political points with public cruelty”.

When a bartender asked James Bond in 2006's Casino Royale whether he'd like his vodka martini shaken or stirred, the irritated spy replied: "Do I look like I give a damn?"
Such throwaway lines were a clever way of signalling to the audience that this was a new era for 007 - and that the film series launched in 1962 was being overhauled with the arrival of Daniel Craig.
Over the next few films, producers struck a balance between nodding to the past while also moving away from some of the cheesier elements of the series, no longer sticking rigidly to all of the tradition and tropes of Bond.
"Were you expecting an exploding pen?" Ben Whishaw's Q later asked the secret service agent in Skyfall. "We don't really go in for that anymore."
Two decades on from Craig's debut, the series is about to be rebooted once again, with a new actor and new creative team. It's an exciting time for Bond fans as they wait to see what shape the next era will take. Here's what we know so far.
Pattinson is known for films including Twilight, The Batman and Tenet
British actor Robert Pattinson has been confirmed as the next actor to play James Bond.
He shot to fame as Cedric Diggory in 2005's Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire, and went on to star in Twilight.
Pattinson appeared opposite Kristen Stewart in the series of five films based on Stephenie Meyers' vampire novels.
He has gone on to star in other major films and franchises including The Batman and Christopher Nolan's recent adaptation of The Odyssey.
But Pattinson is also respected within the industry for his unusual choice of roles, often appearing in independent, arthouse and experimental films.
His other credits include The Lighthouse, Mickey 17, Life, The Drama, Good Time, Primetime, The Rover, Bel Ami, Tenet and The Lost City of Z.
L-R: Callum Turner, Jack Lowden and Jack Barton are all thought to have auditioned for the role
A handful of actors were thought to have made it to the final screen tests before Pattinson scored Britain's biggest film role. They included:
Jack Lowden , 36 - whose credits include Slow Horses and Pride and Prejudice
Josh O'Connor , 36 - The Crown, Wake Up Dead Man: A Knives Out Mystery
But while many of the names are seen as hot, up-and-coming actors, Pattinson was arguably the most bankable movie star.
The film is expected to go into production in 2027, before its release in 2028. No exact dates have been announced.
Film schedules can be notoriously fluid, but it's clear that development is well under way, with the director and writer already in place.
It will be the 26th film in the official film series, but the title has not yet been confirmed.
Steven Knight (left) will write the script, while Denis Villeneuve will direct the film
The movie will be directed by Denis Villeneuve , known for Prisoners, Sicario, Arrival, Blade Runner 2049 and the recent Dune trilogy starring Timothée Chalamet.
"Some of my earliest movie-going memories are connected to 007," the French-Canadian director said last year. "I grew up watching James Bond films with my father, ever since Dr. No with Sean Connery. I'm a die-hard Bond fan. To me, he's sacred territory."
He added: "I intend to honour the tradition and open the path for many new missions to come. This is a massive responsibility, but also, incredibly exciting for me and a huge honour."
Bond 26 will be written by Steven Knight , known for TV series such as Peaky Blinders and House of Guinness, and films including Burnt, Spencer, Locke and The Girl in the Spider's Web.
Knight has said it had always been on his "bucket list" to write a Bond film, adding that he felt he was "doing my duty for King and country" by joining the franchise.
He told the BBC he planned to "write the character, not the actor", adding: "The thing with Bond is it's its own universe and franchise. So there are certain rules.
"Obviously you have to move it along, but I love where it sits. I love that it's British. I love that it's not DC or Marvel... So I feel a responsibility to the text."
Irish actor Pierce Brosnan starred in four Bond films, including 1999's The World Is Not Enough
Sean Connery starred in six official Bond films between 1962 and 1971
Roger Moore starred in seven Bond films between 1973 and 1985
Pierce Brosnan starred in four Bond films, between 1995 and 2002
Daniel Craig starred in five Bond films between 2006 and 2021
That's because Connery returned to the lead role for 1971's Diamonds Are Forever, after Lazenby took his place for 1969's On Her Majesty's Secret Service.
Connery also later appeared in 1983's Never Say Never Again, a Bond film produced by a different studio and not part of the official film series.
If you discount the films not in the official series, there have been 25 Bond films in total. In order, they are:
Daniel Craig (pictured with co-star Léa Seydoux) stepped down as Bond with 2021's No Time To Die
With the change in ownership and a new creative team now in place, the new Bond film is likely to make a fresh start.
It would be difficult to continue the story chronologically given the ending of 2021's No Time To Die, but that still leaves producers with plenty of options.
A different version of James Bond, who exists in a different universe, would be easily pulled off in an era where audiences are used to major film franchises restarting in a different world or timeline.
Bond 26 could even be set in a significantly earlier era - an idea that gained more popularity after Tony Gilroy revealed he and fellow director Steven Soderbergh previously pitched a 1960s version , external of Bond.
Separately, actor Ralph Fiennes recently said , external he had once been in talks to play Bond, and had suggested producers make a "black and white and very sort of film noir-y" version set in the 1950s.
Neither idea materialised, but the suggestion went down well with some Bond fans, who noted a period piece would help make the film truer to Ian Fleming's original character and books.
Exactly what shape the next film takes will become clear at a later stage. For now, Christmas has come early for fans who have been waiting for years to find out who the next 007 will be.
In Robert Pattinson, producers have finally found their spy.
