The director of the Shakespeare Institute has said he will resign if plans to move the centre from Stratford-upon-Avon to Birmingham go ahead.
Professor Michael Dobson said he was "very unhappy" with the University of Birmingham's decision to relocate the postgraduate research institute from its historic home at Mason Croft to the university's Edgbaston campus in September 2027.
"Stratford has been the place where people come to dream of Shakespeare since the 18th Century," he said.
The Shakespeare Institute announced on Facebook on Friday that it had been informed it would leave Stratford after more than 75 years. The future of Mason Croft, along with its historic garden and playing fields, has not yet been confirmed.
The University of Birmingham said the move was "an academic decision" rather than a cost-cutting measure and insisted Shakespeare studies remained a priority.
It said the decision is about the Institute's "long-term future" and "current students, including research students, will be supported individually through the transition".
It added it would consult the Royal Shakespeare Company (RSC), the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust, local representatives and the wider community in the coming weeks.
The Shakespeare Institute was founded in 1951 at the Mason Croft building in Stratford-upon-Avon
However, Dobson rejected the university's characterisation of the decision.
"It affects academics, but it's not an academic decision in which anybody who works on Shakespeare at the University of Birmingham wishes to agree or go along with," he said.
"For 75 years Birmingham has been the only university in the world teaching and studying Shakespeare in Shakespeare's hometown," he said.
"That gives it enormous symbolic capital and has done wonders for the university's visibility and reputation in the humanities."
Dobson said Stratford was "the focus of the world's love of Shakespeare" and claimed the institute helped keep the town on the "intellectual and scholarly map" as well as its tourist and theatrical map.
Professor Michael Dobson says he is "very unhappy" with the University of Birmingham's decision
He also questioned claims the move would help attract students.
"Imagine you've moved your entire life to Stratford-upon-Avon to spend three years writing a thesis using our unique research library, and you're suddenly told the Institute is moving to rooms we haven't even seen in Birmingham.
"It takes a long time to box up, move and reorder 60,000 books."
The RSC said the institute is a "valuable part of what makes Stratford-upon-Avon a thriving town and cultural hub in the heart of the West Midlands".
It added: "We look forward to hearing more about the university's plans, in particular how it will sustain and strengthen its longstanding commitment to specialist Shakespeare teaching and research."
The University of Birmingham said the move to relocate the centre was "an academic decision"
The Shakespeare Institute, which celebrated its 75th anniversary in July, has worked with academics, writers and performers for decades, including Dame Judi Dench.
Meanwhile, a petition calling on the university to reverse its plans has been signed by thousands of people. , external
The campaign urges the university to keep the Institute at Mason Croft, its Grade II listed home since 1951. It also calls for the publication of the rationale, financial figures and equality impact assessments behind the proposal.
Campaigners argue relocating the Institute would damage Stratford's cultural and academic standing and threaten postgraduate Shakespeare studies in a town closely linked to both William Shakespeare and the Royal Shakespeare Company.
The university said the Institute's library "will be kept together as a collection" and "none of it will be disposed" with plans for moving and housing the collection set out "shortly".
It added: "Mason Croft has been the Institute's home since 1951, and we are very mindful of its history.
"No decision has been taken on its future, and it remains the Institute's home for this academic year."

Başrollerini Çağan Efe Ak (Aras), Ata Yaşat (Teoman), Nesrin Cavadzade (Şebnem), Armağan Oğuz (Hakan), Ceren Ayruk (Leyla), Dilara Aksüyek (Nuray) ve Helin Elveren’in (Deniz) paylaştığı dizinin 15 Kasım Pazar akşamı yayınlanan bölümü, Leyla'nın geçmişine ilişkin sarsıcı gerçekleri ve acı yüzleşmeleri gözler önüne serdi.

You've done Liverpool and Scotland proud - Kenny Dalglish on Andy Robertson's career
Andy Robertson has become Scotland's most capped men's international after starting in Monday's Nations League defeat in Switzerland to reach 103 appearances for his country.
Twelve years on from his debut - off the bench in a Poland friendly - he surpassed his friend and fellow Liverpool legend, Kenny Dalglish, whose record haul had stood for 40 years.
After moving level with the man they - and he - will always call King, the Tottenham Hotspur left-back shifted chat towards the former forward, his commendable humility laid bare.
But, in St Gallen, the spotlight shone on one of Scotland's favourite sons as he moves solo at the summit, even if the scoreline was a disappointment.
Robertson set to make history, but hero Dalglish will always be King
For much of this year, Dalglish was the only man to have pulled on the navy blue of Scotland more times than Robertson.
'King Kenny' topped the list on 102 caps - earning his last in November 1986 against Luxembourg when in a player-manager role at Liverpool.
Few since have even come close to toppling him - and Robertson is keen to stress the throne is still reserved for Dalglish - but it is perhaps fitting it is the current captain, given their great friendship.
"He always says: 'You've got millions more games. Nations League, what's that? They didn't have that in my day!'" Robertson joked on the Stick to Football podcast recently.
"I think he might bring up a ratio for years-to-games-played so he's still on top.
"It's obviously something that's been on my radar for a while now. When you get to 80-odd caps, you start to look up."
Dalglish can console himself that his record of 30 goals - held jointly with Denis Law - is safely out of Robertson's reach.
But not out of John McGinn's - the midfielder's double against North Macedonia on Friday took him to within six of the legendary duo.
The Aston Villa captain is lurking only eight caps behind Robertson on the all-time caps list, too, so the Scotland men's centurion club could have three members soon.
Since being given the armband by Alex McLeish after Scott Brown retired in 2018, Robertson has captained Scotland 33 times more than any other player.
At the time, he had earned just 22 caps and was just 24 but had established himself as Liverpool's left-back as they reached the Champions League final.
Now he is the only man to have led Scotland out at three major finals, reaching the milestone at the World Cup this summer.
Scotland and Napoli midfielder Scott McTominay enthused: "He's such a great captain and he's got that good balance between being one of the senior players and saying you need to wake up if you're not playing well.
"Then he's also got the personable side, organising things with the manager, helping young players and stuff. He's brilliant with that, brilliant."
One of those young players is 20-year-old Findlay Curtis, who told the media the night before Robertson's historic night that his captain has "probably been the biggest role model" he's looked up to since joining the international set-up earlier this year.
Perhaps that was because Robertson did him a turn back in the day. Unbeknownst to the skipper.
Rangers winger Curtis was only 14 during the Covid pandemic and was partial to playing a bit of Fifa, and Robertson was a star in his team.
"I was just thinking, I had him in my Fifa team," he explained. "[For] defending and he was just fast as well.
'I had him in my Fifa team!' - Findlay Curtis on going from fan to team-mate of Robertson
Robertson has played under four permanent Scotland team bosses in his 12-year international career.
It was Strachan who plucked him from the under-21s to hand him his debut as a 19-year-old in a win over Poland in March 2014.
McLeish made him captain in 2018, calling Robertson the "outstanding candidate" and an "inspirational figure" - and now he has played five times for new boss Sebastien Pocognoli.
He even played one game under interim manager Malky Mackay in a friendly against the Netherlands at Pittodrie in 2017 as the Scottish FA searched for Strachan's replacement.
However, it is Steve Clarke's seven-year stint that Robertson will be mainly associated with, as the pair led Scotland to three major tournaments.
Robertson played 68 times for Clarke, all of them as captain, and the recently departed head coach consistently praised his figurehead.
"He's been a fantastic captain for Scotland," Clarke said at the World Cup.
"He's worked ever so hard for the country and he leads the group like the leader he is - and he's very, very important to me and the squad."
Over the piece, Robertson's caps are spread fairly evenly among friendlies and qualification games.
Crucially, though, he has also played nine times in major tournaments. What will rankle with him is there is only one win among those nine - June's victory over Haiti in Boston at the World Cup.
Overall, though, Robertson's Scotland career can be characterised by consistency.
He has started 101 of his 103 caps, rarely ever being substituted. He has not missed a camp in three years.
The only question seems to be how many Scotland caps will Robertson end up with?
At 32 and still playing in the Premier League, it appears there will be plenty more to come.

A match that should have been about 103 was instead about four. Andy Robertson is due acclaim for becoming the most capped player in Scotland’s history but how the full-back will wish the moment had arrived in different circumstances.
A second-string Switzerland team pulled Scotland apart, raising further and significant questions about the suitability of Sébastien Pocognoli to carry out the job his paymasters boldly entrusted him with. Scottish FA giddiness about Pocognoli as the successor to Steve Clarke, a hugely successful leader of the national team, is looking increasingly ridiculous. “I don’t think you’ve got time in international football,” said Robertson as dust settled here. Ouch.
This was a horrible night for Pocognoli, who is under serious pressure just three months into his tenure. Scotland’s players looked a disillusioned and disorganised lot. Pocognoli has never previously managed in international football, which renders it reasonable to ask his qualifications to improve this grim scenario. Scotland have finished a distant third in a favourable Nations League section. Ramifications exist for the Euro 2028 qualifying draw in December. Pocognoli is taking a pounding in the court of public opinion.
“The score is painful,” said Pocognoli. “I see a lot of good things in the way that we try to play. The result is heavy but the players gave everything. They enjoy playing like this.” An eye test suggests otherwise. Scotland are overly generous in defence, lame in midfield and powder-puff in attack. It is quite the mix.
Pocognoli’s demeanour during pre-match media duties suggested he was irritated by the early questioning of his approach. The Belgian is unwilling to deviate from the deployment of three centre-backs whether Scotland are at home to North Macedonia or away to Switzerland. While the prospect of facing a highly impressive Swiss team would ordinarily make Scots gulp, there was cause for hope in St Gallen. Not only had Switzerland already won Group B1 but they were in makeshift form.
Switzerland’s lack of cohesion was apparent during an opening spell where the visitors looked decent. A flurry of set pieces and a John McGinn half volley that dipped over Yvon Mvogo’s crossbar emphasised Scottish attacking intent. On a difficult pitch, Switzerland’s first 20 minutes lacked purpose. As good as things were to get for Scotland, alas.
There appeared no real danger as Zachary Athekame fired in a hopeful cross from the Swiss right. Scotland had an abundance of cover inside their own penalty area. The problem was that one of those charged with clearing lines, Lewis Ferguson, instead poked the ball past Angus Gunn. No own goals are pretty; this one was especially ugly. Ferguson had needlessly panicked.
Scotland attempted an immediate response as Aaron Hickey headed wide. The Brentford man had to be withdrawn before the interval, apparently damaging his left hamstring when making a defensive intervention.
Hickey, whose career has been seriously disrupted by injury, was understandably distraught. Although Switzerland were by now in control, McGinn spurned a glorious opportunity five minutes before the interval when heading straight at Mvogo. Adrian Bajrami spared McGinn’s blushes with an even worse miss at the opposite end before the teams headed for their orange wedges. The half had been humdrum in nature.
Ferguson shanking the ball out for a Switzerland corner set the tone for a spell where the game was put firmly out of Scotland’s reach. Samuel Ballet burst forward from midfield before playing a one-two with Remo Freuler and slamming towards the Scotland net. The ball was heading in before Winsley Boteli made certain, with the video assistant referee dismissing Scotland’s appeals for offside. The ease with which Ballet evaded those in navy blue was as striking as the space Freuler found himself in. Scotland’s structure, once a staple, was nonexistent. Five defenders and two deep lying midfielders were being gleefully ignored by the rampaging Swiss.
Number three was another Scotland horror show. Nathan Patterson was dispossessed by Boteli. The forward found Alvyn Sanches, who angled a shot across Gunn. So, so easy. Gunn’s positioning was questionable.
Scott McTominay, again peripheral, slammed over when it looked easier to notch a Scotland consolation. Scottish fans jeered after one sideways pass too many in defence. Many headed for the exit as Zeki Amdouni’s shot deflected off Luke Graham and beyond Gunn.
A year ago, Scotland were celebrating World Cup qualification on the most epic of Hampden Park nights as Denmark were vanquished. It is so difficult to square that occasion with 90 minutes in St Gallen. Scotland look a team in ghastly regression.

Thomas Frank has been confirmed as Crystal Palace’s manager after Pierre Sage was sacked last week. Frank, out of work since being dismissed by Tottenham in February, was quickly identified as Palace’s main target and has signed a two-and-a-half-year deal at the Premier League’s bottom club.
Frank spoke to Palace in the summer about succeeding Oliver Glasner but decided he was not ready to return to the dugout because he wanted to take a break from football.
It is understood that the Dane has also attracted interest from Newcastle and Fulham in recent weeks after difficult starts for Matthias Jaissle and Álvaro Arbeloa respectively. Palace also considered Sean Dyche and Vítor Pereira. The chair, Steve Parish, led negotiations with Frank and assured him funds would be available for players in January. Parish described Frank as “the perfect fit”.

If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.
If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from the iOS App Store on iPhone or the Google Play store on Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.
Palace have conceded 24 goals in their first 10 league games – the worst defensive record in the division – and face Coventry and Hull next, either side of a Europa League meeting with Real Sociedad.
“Crystal Palace is an iconic club in England and in the Premier League,” Frank said. “I will do everything I possibly can to help and support the players and everyone around the place, and I’m really looking forward to meeting them.”
Palace have yet to confirm Frank’s full staff but it is understood Justin Cochrane – an assistant in Thomas Tuchel’s England setup who worked with Frank at Brentford and Tottenham – is expected to join him. There are also talks with Chelsea over Bernardo Cueva, who worked under Frank as Brentford’s set-piece coach before Keith Andrews and is tipped for an assistant’s role at Palace, who said Paddy McCarthy and the goalkeeping coach Andy Quy were staying to work under Frank.
Sage fell out with the Palace hierarchy after a haphazard summer window during which the club signed 11 players but failed to replace Maxence Lacroix, the France defender, adequately. Palace agreed a deal with Club Brugge for Joel Ordóñez but had to pull out of the deal after the Ecuador defender failed a medical owing to a fractured foot. Ordóñez is yet to return to action so they may have to look elsewhere.
The decision to sack Sage was made on Sunday evening but there was no confirmation of his departure until Thursday. Palace sources have insisted the compensation bill for his services is closer to £6m than £10m, partly because the figure they paid up front to Lens to buy him out of his contract in the summer was £2.5m, not £4m, with another £1.5m in bonuses never paid.
Sage held talks with Lens over a potential return but the former Le Havre manager Didier Digard was appointed on Friday. “To all Palace fans, members and players, I just wanted to thank you for the moments we’ve shared,” Sage wrote on X over the weekend. “I wish the club, the team and all of you all the very best! May the club’s colours shine on forever …”

Crystal Palace are Thomas Frank's third London club after previous spells with Brentford and Tottenham
"When the time is right I will look forward to my return as a manager, ready to embrace the job with great energy and dedication," said Thomas Frank in June.
That time is now after the Dane was confirmed as the new manager of Crystal Palace , who are two points and a goal difference deficit away from safety at the bottom of the Premier League.
Former boss Pierre Sage was sacked last week after just 16 league and cup games.
The role offers Frank an opportunity to rebuild his reputation after he was sacked by Tottenham in February after eight months.
Frank described it as "an honour" to be "in charge of this fantastic football club" as Palace announced his arrival on a deal running to June 2029.
" Crystal Palace is an iconic club in England and in the Premier League," Frank told Palace's website.
"I will do everything I possibly can to help and support the players and everyone around the place, and I'm really looking forward to meeting them."
Palace chairman Steve Parish said Frank was the "perfect fit for our club".
But how big is the challenge at Selhurst Park that awaits the man who made his name at Brentford ?
"It's going to be a bit of a shock for Thomas Frank," former West Ham and England goalkeeper Rob Green tells BBC Sport.
"He had his success at Brentford - a very well-run club where players are brought in with a lot of thinking and planning to take over the players they sell for profit.
"They lose players and then have a mad scramble to get players in. They have a team that has been decimated by sales and not replaced by the same quality.
"Thomas Frank needs to find something within that team that builds and garners the belief that means that they can compete in the Premier League, because it feels a long way short of that right now."
Will Frank prove the right fit for Palace and haul the Eagles out of the relegation zone?
Since getting the sack at Tottenham after 26 league games last season, Frank has been out of management longer than he was in charge of Spurs .
In the summer he released a statement in which he said "there have been conversations and opportunities" to return to management, but that he had "decided not to rush into the next role".
Frank's name was heavily linked with Palace before they went for a head coach with no Premier League experience to replace Oliver Glasner - the man who delivered an FA Cup, a Conference League title and the Community Shield before moving to Nottingham Forest .
"Palace had one of the best managers they have had, if not forever, silverware coming across the doorstep. Look at what they achieved last season and instead of building on that, they dismantled a team," said former Tottenham and England goalkeeper Paul Robinson.
Frank once described managing as being on a "hamster wheel" and a "crazy circus". , external
Palace confirmed his coaching staff will include current assistant manager Paddy McCarthy and goalkeeping coach Andy Quy, who previously worked with him at Brentford .
Justin Cochrane, who is part of Thomas Tuchel's England staff, is set to join.
Palace are also in the process of approaching Chelsea set-piece coach Bernardo Cueva, who would join as assistant first-team coach.
It is understood Frank would like to take Andreas Georgson from Tottenham , though the north London club are determined to keep the Swede.
Denmark fitness coach Chris Haslam, who worked with Frank at Tottenham , is another potential member of Palace's new coaching set-up.
So why does Frank feel now is the right moment to return to management at a club propping up the table?
Frank, who was part of BBC Sport's World Cup punditry team during the summer, will be coming into the job refreshed and with renewed energy and enthusiasm following several months out of the game.
Between his appointment as Brentford boss in October 2018 and the sack at Tottenham earlier this year, he managed without a break for seven years and four months.
Spending the past few months away from Premier League pressure has allowed Frank, in his own words, to "study, observe and learn from other leaders both within sport and beyond".
Will his positivity and passion rub off on a Palace team who have lost seven times in 10 top-flight matches?
Frank, who places a major emphasis on set-piece organisation, will have to hit the ground running at Palace, who have lost their past four league games.
They have conceded more goals than anyone else in the Premier League (24) and have scored only 10 themselves.
"If you want someone to go in and restore some stability and defensive solidity while improving the set-piece element of the team, then Thomas Frank is the perfect man for the job," Times football writer Tom Allnutt told BBC Radio 5 Live's Football Daily podcast.
With the Premier League season just 10 games old, Frank certainly has time to turn it around and will have targets in mind when the transfer window opens in January.
Palace sold France centre-back Maxence Lacroix to Chelsea for £52m and Colombia right-back Daniel Munoz to Nottingham Forest for £22m during the summer transfer window.
Allnutt added: "We know they have sold so many good players and so far I don't think they have really replaced them adequately."
Another challenge for Frank is getting midfielder Adam Wharton, who has not played for England since March, back to something like his best form.
After his bruising experience at Tottenham - having established Brentford in the Premier League - Frank has decided to climb back on the hamster wheel with Palace.
" Crystal Palace and Thomas Frank feels like a very good fit," added Robinson.
Thomas Frank has a lot of work to do as Crystal Palace have undoubtedly been the worst team in the Premier League so far this season, ranking bottom not just in points (seven) but also goal difference (-14) and expected goal difference (-8.1).
It's the defence where Frank will have to focus most of his attention. Not only have Palace conceded the most goals (24) but they've also faced the most shots (189) and have the worst expected goals against (xGA) figure in the league (21.9).
Their attack has actually not been too bad. While only Hull have taken fewer shots, the Eagles have created really good chances and have perhaps been unlucky not to score a few more goals given the opportunities they've had.
There is also one significant factor in Frank's favour. Although Palace may be bottom of the Premier League, they are certainly not cut adrift as they sit just two points from safety.
The side propping up the table at this stage have had an average of just three points in the past 10 seasons, but for as bad as they've been, Palace have seven - the most the bottom side have had after 10 games for 24 years.

Vitor Matos spent five years on Jurgen Klopp's staff at Liverpool
Swansea City look to be facing a fight to hold on to Vitor Matos amid serious interest in their head coach from French top-flight club Strasbourg.
Matos is under contract at Swansea until 2030, meaning the Championship side would be due significant compensation should he be lured away.
But that has not stopped Strasbourg targeting the 38-year-old Portuguese, who is due to celebrate a year in charge at Swansea later this month.
Matos' fellow countryman Hugo Oliveira is the current Strasbourg boss, but is under pressure after a run of five defeats in six matches.
Oliveira has managed only three wins in 10 league games since succeeding Gary O'Neil - who left to become Ipswich Town boss – in July.
O'Neil led Strasbourg to an eighth-place finish last season, but they are currently 13th in Ligue 1, only two points above the relegation zone.
Strasbourg are a sister club of Premier League side Chelsea.
Matos has turned Swansea from potential relegation contenders to promotion hopefuls since taking charge, with the club 20th in the Championship when he took over last November.
The Swans finished 11th last season and have made further strides in the first third of this campaign.
Vitor Matos led Swansea to seven wins in their first 10 league games of the season, though they have since lost four in five
Matos' team have been among the early-season pacesetters in the second tier, enjoying two spells on top of the table, but their form has dipped in recent weeks.
Swansea have suffered four defeats in their past five matches, though they remain only three points off top spot going into Saturday's home game against West Bromwich Albion.
Matos was touted as a contender to take charge at Crystal Palace earlier this season - the Eagles have since appointed Thomas Frank - while he has also been linked with a return to Portugal on the back of his impact with the Swans.
Listen to the latest Swansea City interviews, news and discussion on BBC Sounds
When asked in October about the Palace links, Matos said: "I'm Swansea manager. I love being here, love my players, love the staff, so my focus is always on the next game and what we can do better."
In an interview last week, Swansea chief executive Tom Gorringe acknowledged that Matos' impact will not have gone unnoticed at other clubs, though he played down the idea of the former Liverpool coach having his head turned.
"The reality is there'll always be interest in anyone performing well in any role on and off the pitch," Gorringe said.
"That's one of the outcomes of being successful - we're aware of that.
"[But] we're all quite happy. We've all agreed to go on this journey together and we hope that Vitor is here a long time."
After West Brom visit, Swansea go to second-placed Middlesbrough next Tuesday before Cardiff City make the short trip west for the first south Wales derby in two seasons on Sunday, 29 November.

Swansea City are increasingly resigned to their head coach, Vítor Matos, joining Strasbourg after he indicated a desire to join Chelsea’s sister club. The Ligue 1 club have approached Swansea with a view to Matos succeeding Hugo Oliveira.
Strasbourg, acquired by Chelsea’s parent company BlueCo in 2023, have identified Matos as a replacement for Oliveira, who has won three of 10 league matches since succeeding Gary O’Neil in July. The French club are hovering two points above the relegation zone.
Matos is under contract until 2030 and Swansea would be due significant compensation for the 38-year-old, a former Liverpool academy and development team coach.
Matos has won admirers since taking charge of Swansea last November and, despite one win in their past five games, has the south Wales club in the Championship playoff spots. Swansea finished last season in 11th and backed Matos in the transfer market this summer in the hope of pushing on.
Swansea’s next match is at home to West Brom on Saturday, before a trip to Middlesbrough and a south Wales derby against Cardiff in the Welsh capital.
Matos, who is due to celebrate a year in charge at Swansea this month, joined the club from Marítimo, a Portuguese second-division club. His 12-game spell in charge of Maritimo represented his first senior management job.
Strasbourg and Chelsea share a close relationship and have traded players, with Emmanuel Emegha and Valentín Barco joining the English club in recent months.
In the most notable move between the clubs, however, Liam Rosenior left his role as Strasbourg head coach to take charge of Chelsea in January, but the former Hull manager was sacked in April . O’Neil succeeded Rosenior but joined Ipswich in June .

Florian Wirtz scored twice as Germany delivered a 5-0 rout of the Netherlands in Berlin on Monday, reaching the Nations League quarter-finals as group winners.
Brajan Gruda contributed a goal and two assists, with Derry Scherhant and Nico Schlotterbeck also on the scoresheet as the hosts delivered their most impressive display so far under Jürgen Klopp’s leadership.
It was Germany’s biggest win over their neighbours since a 7-0 victory in 1959, and the Netherlands’ first defeat since Xavi Hernández took over as coach in August. The Dutch have still advanced to the last eight by finishing second, with Germany’s fifth goal taking Klopp’s side into top spot.
The visitors had the first good chance when Jurriën Timber found Crysencio Summerville unmarked on the penalty spot, but the winger lost his footing before getting a shot away. Germany then went close as the Berlin native Scherhant hit a post after connecting with a cross from his Freiburg teammate Philipp Treu.
Nine minutes later, Scherhant had another chance from the same spot and this time curled a lovely effort across the face of goal and inside the far post. Germany pushed for more goals after the break, and Wirtz delivered with a superb solo effort on the hour, lifting a shot in off the left post from the edge of the penalty area.
Schlotterbeck headed in from Gruda’s free-kick with 65 minutes gone, and the RB Leipzig winger laid on another goal six minutes later when he tore down the right and found Wirtz, who hammered home from close range. Gruda then added one of his own, tapping in a Scherhant shot which rebounded off a post.
Wirtz said: “We don’t mind who we play. We want to play attacking football. We want to score goals and dominate the opponent. And I think we did that perfectly … We want to keep going next year. We want to get better. I think we’ve taken some great steps in our development as a team.”
“Everyone will go home with a smile on their face – and for at least the next three or four months, no-one will be questioning the German national team,” Klopp said afterwards. “Instead, they’ll be thinking: ‘This could really turn into something.’ We have wonderful footballers, great characters … the lads are even surprising themselves.”
Greece had to settle for third place in Group A2 despite a 1-0 home win over Serbia . Giorgos Masouras scored the second-half winner in Volos, but the hosts missed out on a quarter-final place on head-to-head goal difference, their 7-0 defeat by the Netherlands on Friday proving costly. As group winners, Germany will be seeded in Friday’s draw and will avoid England, France and the winners of Group A4 – probably Portugal – in the last eight.
Switzerland completed a dominant campaign in Group B1 by thrashing Scotland 4-0 in St Gallen . Slovenia finished second in the group, claiming a promotion/relegation playoff place, as Danijel Sturm’s double helped them secure a 3-0 win over North Macedonia .
Max Dowman (pictured) became England Under-21s’ youngest-ever goalscorer by grabbing the late winner in a 3-2 friendly victory over France at Ashton Gate.
Lee Carsley’s side made a lightning start as Tottenham's Mikey Moore gave England an early lead on his first under-21s start. Divin Mubama doubled their lead with a header as Ethan Nwaneri set up both of the hosts' first-half goals.
The Young Lions looked comfortable but Tommy Setford allowed France to pull a goal back after he let Giovani Versini’s cross slip through his fingers. The French winger equalised in style moments later, scoring with a shot from distance.
Carsley had handed a first start to promising Arsenal youngster Dowman and he proved to be the hero, tapping in from Harrison Armstrong's pass to give England the win at only 16 years old. Press Association
In League C, the Faroe Islands beat Moldova 1-0 to complete an unbeaten campaign and earn a playoff place. Slovakia , already guaranteed Group C3 top spot, earned a 2-2 draw with Kazakhstan thanks to Adrian Kapralik’s last-gasp leveller.
Iceland finished Group C4 unbeaten with a 3-0 home victory against Luxembourg securing first place. Second-placed Estonia beat Bulgaria 2-1 to book a playoff spot.
In League D, Gibraltar earned a 1-1 home draw with Malta thanks to Carlos Richards’s late equaliser, while Lithuania defeated Liechtenstein 2-1 in Kaunas.

Former Liverpool full-back Neco Williams has 67 Wales caps, scoring five goals
Wales will be without right-back Neco Williams for their final Nations League group match against reigning champions Portugal on Tuesday (19:45 GMT), while goalkeeper Karl Darlow is a doubt.
Nottingham Forest's Williams has been ruled out after he was injured during Saturday's 3-1 defeat in Norway, while Manchester United's Darlow missed training on Monday and will be assessed further.
Midfielder Ethan Ampadu will also miss out at Cardiff City Stadium because of suspension, but centre-back Ben Cabango and winger Sorba Thomas are available after serving one-match bans.
Wales will finish bottom of Group A4 whatever happens against leaders Portugal, and Craig Bellamy's side will have a relegation play-off in March against one of the League B runners-up for a place in the top tier.
"One or two players had to come off through injury [in Norway]. One or two have come through; one or two haven't," said Bellamy.
"Neco's going to be out. Darlow, we'll wait and see later, and everyone else is fully fit."
With less riding on this fixture than there might have been, Bellamy could be tempted to make further changes to his side from the loss in Oslo.
Cardiff City attacking midfielder Rubin Colwill shone as a substitute, while Bournemouth's David Brooks came off the bench to score an excellent goal.
Colwill's performance was a particularly popular talking point among fans, many of whom have long been calling for the 24-year-old playmaker to feature more regularly for Wales.
"Rubin's been pushing [to start] for a while," said Bellamy. "Once you get this kid in the final third, then he's a player. We've just got to get him in those areas.
"But he's also got to offer us without the ball as well. If you're not good without the ball, you cannot be a top player.
"If you want a lesson tomorrow without the ball, watch Vitinha [Portugal's Paris St-Germain midfielder] if he plays.
"Rubin has moved [up a level] and long may that continue, because if it does Wales have got a brilliant player.
"I'm more harsh on Rubin because I've known him since he was so young, but credit to him and his manager at Cardiff [Brian Barry-Murphy].
"He's helping develop a real player for us that's going to hopefully have a huge impact for the next five to 10 years."

Apple TV'nin casus dizisi Slow Horses'ın sekizinci sezonla biteceği yönündeki söylentiler boşa çıktı. Platform, başrolünde Gary Oldman'ın oynadığı diziye dokuzuncu ve onuncu sezon için onay verdiğini duyurdu. Böylece altıncı sezonu yeni tamamlanan yapımın ekran yolculuğu onuncu sezona kadar uzamış oldu.
Dizinin biteceği beklentisini, Sid Baker karakterini canlandıran Olivia Cooke'un geçen hafta The Times'a verdiği röportaj güçlendirmişti. Cooke, "Son sezonu çekiyorum! Asla asla deme ama bize söylenen bu sanırım ve gerçekten bitiyormuş gibi hissediyoruz. Hepimiz hüzünlü ve dalgınız. Dün makyaj koltuğuna oturdum ve ağladım" demişti.
Variety'nin aktardığına göre Apple, bu sözlerin ardından büyüyen spekülasyonlara dizinin süreceğini açıklayarak yanıt verdi. Yedinci sezonun çekimleri tamamlandı; ekip şu sıralar Londra'da sekizinci sezon için kamera karşısında.

River Cartwright rolündeki Jack Lowden'ın dokuzuncu ve onuncu sezonda yer alıp almayacağı ise bilinmiyor. Jurgen Klopp’s side outclasses the Dutch 5-0 in Berlin to secure the top spot in UEFA Nations League Group A2.
An impressive Germany swept aside off-colour Netherlands 5-0 in Berlin to pip the Dutch to first place in UEFA Nations League Group A2.
Germany needed a win to stand a chance of reaching the quarterfinals, starting the night in third place behind Greece, who had won 1-0 in Germany in September, by virtue of their head-to-head record.
Jurgen Klopp’s side produced a fine attacking display to inflict the heaviest defeat on the Dutch in 67 years, as Xavi Hernandez’s side looked very ragged as they shipped four goals in 17 second-half minutes.
Greece’s win over Serbia left the top three sides level on 11 points, but Germany took the top spot on head-to-head while the Dutch finished second, qualifying for the last eight on goal difference thanks largely to their 7-0 win over Greece on Friday.
After a quiet opening 20 minutes, Kai Havertz headed straight at keeper Bart Verbruggen from a Joshua Kimmich free-kick, while Donyell Malen headed a Cody Gakpo cross from the left of the area over the bar from close range soon after.
Berlin-born Derry Scherhant fired a half-volley against the outside of the Dutch post on 32 minutes after collecting a cross from the right byline, but it turned out to be a range-finder as Scherhant scored his first international goal from a similar position on 44 minutes. After cutting in from the left of the area and working space, he flashed an unstoppable shot past Verbruggen and into the far top corner.
Scherhant almost grabbed his second a minute after the interval as he jinked and bundled his way through on goal on the left of the area only to lash a left-footed effort over the bar with only Verbruggen to beat.
Denzel Dumfries headed over the bar at the other end after running onto a bouncing cross at the back post after ghosting past Scherhant on 48 minutes. Meanwhile, the lively Brajan Gruda came close to a spectacular second at the other end after some neat control and cutting in from the right before flashing a shot past the upright from the edge of the Dutch box.
Soon after, Gakpo tested ter Stegen with a low strike from outside the box, but Germany made him pay as Florian Wirtz doubled the lead with a stunning strike into the top corner from the edge of the D with his left foot on the hour.
Nico Schlotterbeck glanced home a header from Gruda’s curling free-kick from the left within five minutes to make it 3-0, and the fourth arrived soon after as Gruda was allowed to glide into the area on the right and get to the byline before dinking the ball back into the middle for the unmarked Wirtz to lash home his second goal with a volley off the underside of the bar.
Gruda nearly added a goal to his two assists as his rising shot was stopped by Verbruggen after another silky run, but the 22-year-old eventually marked his second cap with his second international goal on 77 minutes when he fired home the rebound after Scherhant’s shot came back off the inside of the post.
It led to Verbruggen calling an impromptu huddle outside his area as the visitors sought to end their misery, and they saw the game out without further alarm.
Germany will be seeded in Friday’s draw for the last eight, which will be contested over two legs in March.

Thomas Tuchel believes winning the Nations League would provide England with the springboard to Euro 2028 glory. The head coach watched his team close out the calendar year with a sensational 3-2 victory against Spain at the Metropolitano Stadium on ­Sunday.
It meant England leapfrogged the world champions to finish top of their Nations League group and ensured seeded status for the ­quarter-final draw on Friday. England will co‑host the European Championship and Tuchel wants to go into it as the Nations League winners.
“It is for me and for us,” he said when asked about the importance of the Nations League and its potential to help a team to bigger and better things. “I saw and heard about the celebrations in Portugal when they won it last year [beating Spain on penalties in the final]. It is just the best preparation we can have for the Euros. We don’t think so far, but it’s a fact.
“We want to have these matches on the highest level to prove ourselves, to gain in confidence and to see where we are … to adjust our game where we need a bit of adjustment. That’s what this Nations League is perfect for. We want to win it. But first of all, we need to win the quarter-final.”
The defender Ezri Konsa echoed Tuchel’s thoughts. “The Nations League is a trophy and silverware going into the Euros would be ­massive for us,” he said. “We want to win the Euros and we know it is on home soil. That will give us a ­massive boost.”
England surged into a 3-0 lead against Spain only to have Elliot Anderson sent off in the 63rd minute when he conceded a penalty. Mikel Oyarzabal scored it and the closing stages were nervy for England. There were shades of the World Cup semi-final defeat against Argentina as England sought desperately to defend their advantage.
“Playing with 10 men against the world champions would be difficult,” Konsa said. “The amount of balls coming into the box we dealt with really well.
“The World Cup has gone. We have passed that. We are focused on winning each game and we know we have the Euros coming up.
Max Dowman (pictured) became England Under-21s’ youngest-ever goalscorer by grabbing the late winner in a 3-2 friendly victory over France at Ashton Gate.
Lee Carsley’s side made a lightning start as Tottenham's Mikey Moore gave England an early lead on his first under-21s start. Divin Mubama doubled their lead with a header as Ethan Nwaneri set up both of the hosts' first-half goals.
The Young Lions looked comfortable but Tommy Setford allowed France to pull a goal back after he let Giovani Versini’s cross slip through his fingers. The French winger equalised in style moments later, scoring with a shot from distance.
Carsley had handed a first start to promising Arsenal youngster Dowman and he proved to be the hero, tapping in from Harrison Armstrong's pass to give England the win at only 16 years old. Press Association
“It’s very important to end the year on a high. You end it with huge confidence going into next year’s set of games. We are taking it camp by camp. But going into March [and the Nations League quarter-finals] we will have a lot of confidence.”
Tuchel said: “We took the next steps after the World Cup and I’m very proud of the performance against Spain. It’s a real statement victory. It was the way we won; the way we played the third phase was very impressive. You could see the steps we take between every single match.”

Thomas Frank returns to the Premier League with Crystal Palace after being sacked by Tottenham in February; he will replace Pierre Sage at Selhurst Park; Palace are bottom of the table with just seven points from their first 10 games
Crystal Palace have appointed Thomas Frank as their new manager.
The Dane replaces Pierre Sage, who was dismissed on November 12 following a seventh league defeat of the season to Liverpool.
Frank has signed a deal until the summer of 2029 - and took charge of his first training session as Palace boss on Monday.
Palace chairman Steve Parish said of Frank: "He has a proven track record of both creating winning teams and improving players making him the perfect fit for our club.
"I'm confident Thomas' extensive experience in the Premier League will help us achieve our goals for the rest of the season."
Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player
Frank was among a list of names that Palace considered in the summer before Sage was appointed to the role.
Other candidates that Palace were interested in included Frank Lampard , Sean Dyche , Vitor Pereira , Kim Hellberg , Vitor Matos, Tony Popovic, Jens Berthel Askou and Ole Werner.
Frank added: "It's an honour to sit here and be in charge of this fantastic Football Club. I'm really, really looking forward to it.
"Crystal Palace is an iconic club in England and in the Premier League. I will do everything I possibly can to help and support the players and everyone around the place, and I'm really looking forward to meeting them."
Frank had great success at Brentford during his seven-year spell between 2018 and 2025, getting the Bees into the Premier League and then establishing them as a top-flight club, reaching a ninth-place finish in 2023.
He then moved to Tottenham last season to replace Ange Postecoglou, but was sacked after less than eight months in charge with the club in 16th place, five points above the relegation zone.
Spurs only sealed survival from relegation on the final day of last season, by which stage Roberto De Zerbi was head coach.
Frank failed to win over the Tottenham faithful, with his short tenure littered with setbacks, including drinking from a coffee cup which carried the badge of rivals Arsenal.
Palace are bottom of the Premier League with seven points, two from safety. They face the team in 17th place - Coventry - when the league resumes on Saturday.
They are also 21st in the Europa League table - which would currently see them through to the knockout play-off phase - with one win, two draws and one loss so far. The Eagles face Real Sociedad - a place ahead of them on goal difference - at Selhurst Park in their next European fixture on November 26.
Frank was Crystal Palace's No 1 choice to take over from Sage.
Palace believe their squad is much better than their current position in the Premier League table.
Frank is believed to be rejuvenated and refreshed after taking some time away from the game, having recently returned from Australia.
His first task is to get Palace out of the relegation zone, with the club two points from safety.
The Dane's willingness to use a variety of formations could be a key factor in bringing the best out of Palace's current squad.
Frank was also interviewed for the Manchester United and Chelsea jobs in the summer of 2024.
Two members of Frank's backroom team have already been announced.
Current assistant manager Paddy McCarthy is staying on, alongside goalkeeper coach Andy Quy , who coincidentally worked with Frank at Brentford.
However, Palace are working on putting together Frank's coaching team.
They are approaching Chelsea to get Bernardo Cueva . He was a set-piece coach under Frank at Brentford before moving to Chelsea - but Cueva would work as a coach at Palace.
Palace also want to add Justin Cochrane to Frank's coaching team. The two worked together at Brentford and Spurs and Cochrane is currently part of Thomas Tuchel's England coaching team.

As he prepares to depart for Manchester United, the outgoing US coach held court on a number of topics, including what he’d change about soccer in America
O utgoing US head coach Mauricio Pochettino and former Manchester City head coach Pep Guardiola have a long, storied past. The two faced each other as players, when Guardiola was at Barcelona and Pochettino was making his name across town at Espanyol. They faced each other 22 times as managers in the Premier League and the two share a mutual respect – and intensity – when it comes to their approach to playing and coaching alike.
So when Guardiola visited Yankee Stadium in September to serve as New York City FC’s pre-match hype man before their rivalry match with Red Bull New York, Pochettino – in town anyways to scout the match – made it a point to sit with him during the game. He brought along his assistant coach and confidant Jesús Pérez, and US Soccer CEO and secretary general JT Batson.
“You know what I noticed?” Pochettino asked, smiling as he recounted the story during a meeting with reporters on Monday. “[Guardiola had a] good relationship with JT.”
Back then, Pochettino didn’t seem to be going anywhere. Only a month earlier, he’d signed a four-year contract to guide the US through the 2030 World Cup. Guardiola was, and still is, in the middle of a year-long sabbatical from coaching. He remains the federation’s white whale, often mentioned in the same breath as the US job over the past decade-plus but just as quickly dismissed as a pipe dream.
Just three months after taking in that game at Yankee Stadium, Pochettino is on his way to Manchester United and Guardiola has once again found himself at the center of the rumor mill, with reports suggesting that he and US Soccer are set for exploratory talks.
On Monday, Pochettino was asked what he’d tell the Barcelona and Manchester City legend if he was asked for his opinion on the US job.
“Take it,” Pochettino said, flatly. “Why? Because it’s a perfect moment to arrive at the federation. Everything is on the right path, in the right direction. Of course, take it. Of course, you are going to find really good players, good people – the players can fit his style.”
Guardiola was one of many topics the Argentinian manager covered during the roundtable, which lasted about an hour. At times defiant, at times emotional and cycling through Spanish and English, Pochettino spoke of his potential legacy at US Soccer, what lies ahead for him at United and how he views soccer in America as a whole.
However you assess his results, one of the inarguable successes of the Pochettino era are the relatively unheralded players whose status has risen over his tenure. The Argentine cited defender Alex Freeman and midfielder Sebastian Berhalter as two such examples, both of whom were playing in MLS when making their national team debuts under Pochettino and both now playing in Europe. Asked how he assesses players to add to the national team, and how he compares players across different leagues and playing styles, Pochettino insisted that the level of competition matters less than individual form.
“You need to project the individual player,” Pochettino said. “Because he’s playing well, the level is no issue. That player can be good, like Freeman, like Sebastian. That is the example, and I think that is so important. There is talent everywhere … This one is one of the things that we learn – all [of us], we were young and then we start to be a coach, no? That we cannot make a mistake [and] measure the level of the player because of the level of the league.”
With the US being his first international job, there were some doubts going in about how Pochettino would adapt to coaching without daily contact with his players and staff.
“I am ready [to return]. This is what I miss a little bit. I miss to be, every day, with something here,” Pochettino said. “Guardiola asked me when I was at the game, he said, ‘Oh, you don’t want to come back to the Premier League?’ I said, ‘No, I’m happy here.’ [He said] ‘Yeah, but you don’t miss, every day, to…’ I say, ‘A little bit, yes, because you think now today, and then we have December camp against Jamaica for the MLS [players in the pool]. But after, you need to wait [until] March. What do you do? You need to watch games, you need to travel – administrative things. That is nice, it’s good. But every day, to be involved: press conference, training, everything … this type of possibility, like with United, you say yes. I want that. I want to prove myself again.”
But what did Pochettino think of his maiden international job?
“I like and not like,” he said. “I like because it provides you the possibility to manage your time, to be busy, but at the same time, be free and to have some time with your family. Now, I have a grandchild, and [number] two is coming. You can share the life with your people. But now, ciao, because now is [gestures] tra-tra-tra-tra-tra . It’s impossible to spend time with the people you want.”
In the grand scheme of international football, the US national team coaching job has never been close to the top of the list of most desirable destinations. Pochettino’s hire was seen as a possible sign that could be changing. Now, after nearly two years in the position, Pochettino believes it has.
“The vision from Europe, I promise it is completely different after the World Cup,” Pochettino said. “Now, being head coach of the USA is more prestigious. If Manchester United, or Real Madrid, or Barcelona is coming for the US coach, if you start to think about that, if you are another coach – maybe [Antonio] Conte, someone else, you say ‘oh, this is a great opportunity.’ [In my case], ‘Oh, Pochettino, from Chelsea he goes to the US? And now to Manchester United.’
Pochettino has coached some of the most famous players and clubs in the world, giving him a unique perspective on how soccer has developed in the US. Pochettino stopped short of prescribing neat solutions to improve the sport, though.
“I think that business [and] the sport, is [done] in a holistic way. Everything is important, and you cannot pick one. You cannot change one [thing], and that can change everything,” he said. “I think it’s a little bit of everything that you need to change. If you adjust this, you need to adjust this. The balance of the thing changes if you touch here, that will force you to touch all the areas in soccer here, or in the world To find the good balance, no? A process of little by little, is all that we made in these last two years. I think it’s the beginning of [a process]. If that has continuity, it’s the beginning of the new soccer in the USA that can be.
“I think that is, for me, the beginning of the change for the future: that idea that the American player can be very good, can be very competitive. The talent is here; it’s so powerful in this country. I think that is why I feel proud. Maybe that was our job, because I don’t believe in coincidence. That has happened because something needed to happen. Now the tough job is done. Maybe now [the United job] is my reward because of this tough job.”

Jorge Jesus has responded to claims by Cristiano Ronaldo's mother, Dolores Aveiro, that her son had been "deceived" by the Portugal manager.
Ronaldo, 41, retired from international football on 5 November, ending a career with his country during which he won 234 caps and scored 146 goals.
But his retirement also came less than a month after he had been given a 30-day suspension and fined £215 for walking out of the Portugal camp in September after being told he would not start the Nations League match against Denmark.
Portugal played their first game since Ronaldo's announcement against the Danes on Saturday, losing 4-1 at home .
While attending a Sporting event on Monday, Aveiro was asked about Ronaldo's national team retirement, and said: , external "Of course he was sad.
"They deceived him. And I'm sad, too. The defeat [against Denmark] was well-deserved. I was actually glad."
Before Portugal's Nations League game against Wales in Cardiff on Tuesday (19:45 GMT), Jesus was asked for his thoughts on Aveiro's comments.
"Now I have to respond to Cristiano Ronaldo's mother?" he said.
"She is a lady I greatly respect - she suffered a lot to raise her children."
Asked if the debate about Ronaldo's international retirement would end, Jesus added: "I don't know when it's going to stop.
"If you guys ask the questions, I have to answer. If you ask about Ronaldo next year, I will answer."

Wales take on Portugal in the Nations League on Tuesday, with the visitors without Cristiano Ronaldo in Cardiff after his retirement; Ben Davies is pretty pleased the legendary forward is not in the Portugal squad - with Craig Bellamy unmoved by the whole saga
The Cardiff City Stadium sold out very quickly when the Nations League fixtures threw up a Wales vs Portugal game for the final match of Group D.
Mark the date, November 17, 2026 - it could have been the last time to see Cristiano Ronaldo play on UK soil.
A mouthwatering occasion to witness one of the greats of the game as the curtain slowly falls on his illustrious international career and also see just how far Wales are progressing after a full campaign in League A of the Nations League, a full campaign among the heavyweights of European football.
As we all know, that's not how it's panned out! After Ronaldo's appearance against Wales in Lisbon at the start of the Nations League, he's not featured since - and he's now called time on his Portugal career amid some controversy.
Even though Ronaldo's not here in Wales and the ending of his Portugal days were perhaps not the best scripted, he'll certainly be missed by many. Wales manager Craig Bellamy for one: "As soon as he retires then suddenly like, it's all hell breaks loose!
Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player
"He is one of the best players that has ever played the game. We are all going to miss him. Now, he's still playing club football, so we still get little bits to watch him.
"So just be grateful you got to see an incredible talent that you can call yours, and this is me speaking to Portuguese people. But I'm grateful that we got to see the longevity of a true great, who's had one of the biggest impacts in football in general and will go on to have a big impact by just the young kids who watch him.
"I feel it's like stop the talking now. Just celebrate. Celebrate. I'm grateful I got to see him and I'm grateful I got to coach against him as well."
Wales captain Ben Davies offered a wry smile and an alternative view of Ronaldo's retirement, from an opposition player's perspective: "Any game where you probably don't play against Cristiano Ronaldo, I think it's sometimes better for you…" That's Davies at his most understated!
He added: "You're not too concerned of what he can do to you on that day, he's a world-class player. It's been an honour and a privilege to share the pitch with him because of what he's done in the game. We were lucky to do that in Lisbon, but there won't be too many players in Wales complaining that he's not going to be there."
Despite the Wales-Portugal fixture having implications for both countries, more questions were asked about Ronaldo than perhaps most others. Welsh, British and Portuguese reporters were all guilty at some point of asking media questions about the missing No 7.
Take away the circus that followed and still follows Ronaldo, so many Wales fans thought about buying a ticket and coming along to watch Ronaldo strut his stuff and to also show their appreciation, that it's actually difficult to ignore Ronaldo's absence from their perspective.
Fans pay good money to watch elite sport and many had hoped a farewell to Ronaldo was part of the entrance fee. A great shame for nigh on 35,000 inside the Cardiff City Stadium on Tuesday night.
What the crowd will get though is a Portugal side packed with talent - the quality and depth of their squad on paper is ridiculous.
But it's a squad that has come to Cardiff slightly reeling from a very unexpected home thrashing at the hands of Denmark who beat them 4-1 at the weekend.
Is this what Portugal will be like without Ronaldo? I doubt it… but Wales have a free shot at Portugal, their League A campaign has only mustered one win, but bar a drab home game against Denmark, Bellamy's side have gone toe to toe with Portugal and Norway.
There have been "moments" as Bellamy ruefully alluded to in all matches where Wales have produced quality and consistency beyond their opponents. It's brought a victory over Norway, but in the other four games Wales have just been short. Short, but at least trying.
Even the most ardent Wales supporter who is not a "Bellamy" fans (and there a few) can't talk away some plain stats. Wales have enjoyed decent possession in all their League A games and create chances - 12 against Norway last Saturday. Perhaps one link missing is an out and out goalscorer where chances created and shots at goal actually turn into 'goals'.
For Bellamy this League A campaign has been fruitful IF you can look beyond the short term: "You want to be exposed to the profile of teams we've been exposed to. It's beyond motivating to play these teams and even the moments that don't go your way, you learn, you know? Like that killer moment.
"You can't get away with anything, can you? At the moment, we've got in, we're side-netting (not the goal), so it's the difference. I thought we definitely brought a good version of ourselves to these games, we've definitely been competitive in these games and I expect us to be competitive, but it's just final moments, those final details.
"Are we creating opportunities to score? Well, xG is higher than what we're converging so that's telling you we're creating big opportunities.
"They're the moments that can turn what you feel is a good performance into actually coming away and winning these type of games and I believe the best way you're able to do that is by playing against them on a regular basis, by being in that position.
"So yeah, we're desperate to stay in Group A. We want to stay in this league, it motivates us a lot to stay in this league."
Bellamy's Wales will finish bottom of their group, but their record is better than many other teams in League A such as Czech Republic, Serbia and Turkey so they will not be automatically relegated.
A play-off awaits Wales next March against a League B runner-up. Wales will take that and fancy their chances especially with the home leg second.
With Euro 2028 the longer term aim, remaining in League A the medium term aim, the short term is to do a Wales 'rugby'.
Defy the pundits and 'superior' opposition and create a result and performance that many people talk about for years to come and say to one another; "I was there… even if Ronaldo wasn't."

Martin Tyler's new book 'Tales from the Gantry: Letters from a Lifetime in Football' was published on Monday; the legendary ex-Sky Sports commentator has backed England to win their first major trophy since 1966 at the 2028 Euros on home soil after Sunday's 3-2 Nations League win in Spain
Martin Tyler is more convinced than ever he will finally get the chance to commentate on England winning a major international trophy after watching Thomas Tuchel's side's 3-2 Uefa Nations League victory in Spain
The legendary football commentator, whose new book 'Tales from the Gantry: Letters from a Lifetime in Football' was published on Monday, knows a thing or two about England teams, good and bad, having called over 350 Three Lions internationals while attending an astonishing 13 World Cup finals during a decorated 53-year career that is still going today.
The book is "historical", says Tyler. "It is what I was thinking about in football that week. There's 110 different essays, half a dozen of them were letters from America.
"I wrote 500 words a week for two and a half years. It starts early in 2004 and finishes in July 2026."
Tyler's illustrious career began back in December 1974 commentating for ITV region Southern Television, then Yorkshire Television and Granada, while he was chosen to call the 1982 World Cup final alongside Ian St John before joining BSkyB [the sports arm of which became Sky Sports in 1991] in 1990.
And it was there where for the next 33 years, he became the voice of football for so many, commentating on many of the most unforgettable and dramatic games in that time.
"It'll be 52 years in December," Tyler recalls, almost himself taken aback by the longevity of his career.
"It's extraordinary, really. Talk about time going fast when you're having fun and I've had a lot of fun. Time has gone very fast!
"Then the Premier League came along and the rest is history…."
Undoubtedly, Tyler's most memorable piece of Premier League commentary came at the Etihad Stadium in May 2012 when Manchester City scored twice in stoppage time to be crowned champions for the first time in 44 years after beating Queen's Park Rangers to win the Premier League on goal difference from arch-rivals Manchester United.
"AGUEROOOOO!" Tyler exclaimed as the Argentine's late strike hit the net to send the Etihad into delirium. "I swear you'll never see anything like this ever again! So, watch it, drink it in."
Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player
Looking back now, Tyler is happy with how one of the most played pieces of football commentary in this country came out.
"I think my statement still holds good and basically, it's the football you respond to, we don't create anything as commentators, we react to it, it's a reactive job and we try and find the right words at the right time," he says.
"And sometimes you do, and sometimes you don't, and when I think about that particular game you're referring to, it might have been a different story if I hadn't come up with the words, but I managed to do it, it was one of my good days."
Speaking of good days, well that is exactly what England had in the Spanish capital on Sunday night as the visitors inflicted a first defeat on the world and European champions in two years and 43 matches in what Tyler labelled a near-faultless display.
"That was a very impressive England performance," he says. "For an hour, it was almost perfection. And then, of course, it became what 11 against 10 should be, but isn't always. To be fair to Spain, they came up with some really important questions that England had to deal with."
One player in particular caught Tyler's eye at the Wanda Metropolitano.
"We talk a lot about Old Trafford, we should be talking about young Trafford now," he added. "I think that will be seen as the day where he announced whether he would replace Jordan Pickford as a fine goalkeeper.
"Immediately, I don't know, but he has proved that he is capable of being England's No 1 as Jordan's career will, obviously, because of the difference in age, will not exactly peter out, because he won't let that happen.
"But he will realise that there's some serious competition and that's what happens in life, you know. You have your run, and then somebody comes and says, 'I'll have a bit of that' and undoubtedly, England wouldn't have won the game without him."
In fact, so impressive were England for an hour in Madrid that Tyler feels he is now not far away from the thrill of commentating on England finally getting their hands on a major piece of silverware for the first time since 1966.
"I would love to do that," he says. "The best I can do is the under-18s when Gary Neville was playing, back in 1993, which we covered on Sky Sports. So that's as close as I've come.
"I've seen England go out at pretty much every World Cup since anyone can remember really. I've certainly seen England go out, even in 1954, 1962 and 1966 as a television watcher, although I went to a game in '66.
"And 1970, I remember walking out, I was still living with my parents, into the streets going, 'how did we manage to lose that?' We were the holders, which made it even more painful!
"England are looking capable of winning. I really hope that they can win the Nations League because I rate the Nations League as a tournament. England came, we forget, third in the first one.
"I can't honestly say looking at that first half last night, I can't believe that any international team in the world would have coped with that kind of performance.
"That was top of the range and the way in modern football where press is everything, they squeeze the life out of the world champions. It didn't win them the match as such because of what happened afterwards, they needed other elements like James Trafford to make sure we did win the game, but it's exciting times for England.
"The expression is you can't win them all, but it would be nice to win one. I'm sure we will. I'm really convinced. Last night, I was watching and I thought, 'this team will win something' and that's obviously a golden opportunity coming up here in the next Euros."
Tyler, now 81, still hopes to be commentating on the European championship in 2028 when he may finally get that chance to describe England captain Harry Kane walking up the Wembley steps to lift the Henri Delaunay Trophy.
"As you get older, I would say this to everybody past a certain age, don't retire," he says. "Keep things in your life!"
And what better way to hang up the microphone after more than half a century commentating than to call England's major trophy win for 62 years.

Match report as Scotland lose to Switzerland in their final Nations League Group B1 match; Lewis Ferguson's own-goal put the hosts ahead; Winsley Boteli, Alvyn Sanches and Zeki Amdouni scored in the second half; Scotland will remain in League B for the next Nations League tournament
Andy Robertson created Scotland history, then delivered a scathing assessment of their Nations League collapse against Switzerland.
On the night he became the men's record appearance holder with 103 caps, Sebastien Pocognoli came under pressure with a bruising 4-0 defeat in St Gallen.
"That cannot happen in international football," he told BBC Scotland after the match.
"I don't think you've got time in international football, you have to do it. These supporters who travel everywhere, are they going to give us time? No. Are the people inside Hampden going to give us time? No. Are the people outside Hampden, who are going to be critical and rightly so? No.
"We don't have time, the players do not have time, we have got to step up.
"We have a long break now to March, which is not a good thing, and it is going to be a tough one to swallow."
The Scots were comfortable against the much-changed Group B1 winners until the 22nd minute when midfielder Lewis Ferguson put through his own goal.
The unforced error deflated the visitors, who lost wing-back Aaron Hickey to injury before the break, and there was more damage in the 47th minute when Samuel Ballet's drive was touched in by Winsley Boteli before Alvyn Sanches hammered in a third just four minutes later, with substitute Zeki Amdouni adding a late fourth.
The Scots finished third in the group behind Switzerland and Slovenia, with seven points from 18, missing out on a promotion play-off spot next year and a more favourable seeding for the European Championship qualifying draw next month.
The Belgian boss' first campaign as Steve Clarke's successor has been underwhelming to say the least with just two wins - both against bottom side North Macedonia - from six fixtures and Pocognoli now finds himself under the spotlight just months into his tenure.
2: SAVE! A comfortable save for Angus Gunn but Isaac Schmidt is given too much time to get a shot away. An early warning.
17: CHANCE! John McGinn hooks the ball over the bar as Scotland continue to pile on the pressure.
22: GOAL SWITZERLAND! Disaster for Scotland as Lewis Ferguson sticks out his leg and sends the ball into his own net.
24: CLOSE! Almost an equaliser from Aaron Hickey. He gets his head to Andy Robertson's cross, but it's just past the post.
36: INJURY! Hickey pulls up holding his hamstring and his night is over.
42: CHANCE! Nathan Patterson sends the ball in to McGinn but he heads straight at the goalkeeper. An opportunity missed.
44: CHANCE! That should be a second for Switzerland! Adrian Bajrami gets on the end of the cross but somehow heads the ball well off target.
47: GOAL SWITZERLAND! Samuel Ballet plays a one-two with Remo Freuler, and Winsley Boteli gets the last touch to put the Swiss two up.
51: GOAL SWITZERLAND! Alvyn Sanches gets on the end of a ball from Boteli and fires across Gunn and into the net.
66: SAVE! Gunn pulls off a save to deny Ballet a fourth for the hosts and Luke Graham is there to block Zeki Amdouni's follow-up effort.
72: OVER! Scott McTominay gets on the end of Kieran Tierney's cross and somehow blasts it over the bar.
85: SUB! Kristi Montgomery replaces Ferguson as he makes his Scotland debut.
89: GOAL SWITZERLAND! Amdouni's shot from the edge of the box takes a deflection off Graham as it goes past Gunn.
Almost a year on from the elation of Scotland beating Denmark to reach the World Cup, it now looks like a struggle to reach Euro 2028.
Scotland will be in Pot 3 when the draw is made next month, and there is a lot of improvement needed before the qualifying campaign then kicks off in March.
In his first six games as Steve Clarke's successor, Sebastien Pocognoli has won just two. Both against North Macedonia.
They had a decent first 20 minutes in St Gallen, but this was not Switzerland's best team.
Murat Yakin was without Granit Xhaka, Dan Ndoye, Manuel Akanji and Johan Manzambi and they still made it look easy against the Scots who managed just one shot on target. A tame one.
How much time should the new Scotland head coach bet given? Following the man who led the nation to three major tournaments was always going to be a hard act to follow, but the team appears to have regressed.
Scotland head coach Sebastien Pocognoli speaking to BBC Scotland:
"The score is heavy with the 4-0, but I don't think it's a reflection of the game, if I'm really honest and objective.
"I think we had some very good moments in the game, we started the game like we wanted, aggressive away from home.
"I think if we were in confidence, we would not produce the moments we produce in the game.
"I think we create good moments on the ball, on pure bravery decisions to play forward through the lines or the pressure.
"We create chances also for pressing, sometimes we should have to manage better the transition from pressing, but it is all the things we want to see.
"So the next step is to have the quality to just finish this action, and the more we have games together, the more we will try to fix these things.
"We have a lot of good response from this camp and it's good for the future as well."
"First half we were in the game but lost a stupid goal. But I thought we had chances and should have made it one each at half-time.
"We talked about it at half-time, we told ourselves to keep going and the time you get to 50 minutes, you're 3-0 down? That cannot happen in international football.
"That's what happened tonight. We were playing against a good team. But while we were in the game in the first half, you have to do it for 90 minutes. Then you're 3-0 down, it's a tough place to come and that. A really tough night for us."
